Business.title: Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation
Business.text:
Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation.

The cost of a barrel of oil jumped 6% to above $107 on Thursday amid concerns that advances by Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast in Yemen could choke off Saudi crude exports.

The global bond sell-off that has rocked markets in recent weeks resumed in response to the news from the Middle East – which came against a backdrop of escalating concern about out-of-control government borrowing.

Higher oil prices, which had already climbed since hostilities resumed in the Iran war, are expected to drive up inflation, prompting central banks to raise interest rates and putting the brakes on economic growth.

Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the conflict with Iran could continue until “immediately after” November’s US midterm elections, at which point he claimed oil prices would be “tumbling downward”.

The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, with its president, Christine Lagarde, saying: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated.”

“The conflict in the Middle ​East continues ​to ⁠generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to ​remain well above target for ​an ⁠extended period,” she added.

As Thursday’s sell-off gathered pace in London, the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds surged above 5.37% – the highest cost of borrowing since 2007 – creating a fresh headache for the new chancellor, John Healey.

With less than seven weeks to go until Healey’s first budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on the UK’s debt-pile will raise the cost of future investment projects and eat into the Treasury’s fiscal headroom.

At the same time, the prospect of higher energy bills as oil and gas prices rise is likely to intensify pressure on the government to help consumers to weather the winter.

Unleaded petrol prices have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the motoring organisation the RAC, while the prospect of higher inflation has prompted some banks to raise their mortgage rates.

Healey has promised to provide a “breathing space” for UK households while also addressing the cost of doing business.

In a speech on Monday, however, he also sought to tame bond market fears by committing himself to “controlling borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”.

In the US, where Trump has promised to write a $5,000 (£3,700) cheque for every adult citizen if the Republicans win the midterms, Thursday’s sell-off pushed up the yield on 10-year borrowing to 4.92% – the highest since 2023.

The cost of longer-term borrowing also continued to surge, with 30-year yields hitting the highest level since 2007, despite the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, intervening directly in debt markets on Wednesday.

Bessent hoped to bring down yields by buying back $6bn worth of government debt; but investors appeared to respond by deepening the sell-off.

Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at the broker Capital.com, said: “Ultimately, a sustained drop in long-end yields can ​only be achieved by genuine shifts in macroeconomic policy: ​either the US government pulling back on spending or the ​Fed lifting rates.”

Policymakers at the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, will meet under its new chair, Kevin Warsh, to set interest rates next week.

Markets are expecting a rise – potentially enraging Trump, who has repeatedly demanded rate cuts. In a TruthSocial post last week, the president said: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.”

A plethora of UK data to be published over the next week, including on inflation, jobs and growth, will give an updated snapshot of how resilient the British economy has been in the face of the Iran war.

In the first six months of the year, UK growth was the strongest among the G7 economies. This was despite higher-than-expected oil prices and the absence of hoped-for rate cuts.

Bank of England policymakers will also meet next week, but are expected to leave the UK’s key interest rate on hold at 3.75% for the time being as they continue to monitor the impact of higher oil prices.

Business.title: ECB raises interest rates to 2.5% and warns Iran war is fuelling inflation
Business.text:
The European Central Bank has raised interest rates to 2.5% and warned that the risk of higher inflation over the next year has risen following renewed fighting in the Middle East.

It came as government borrowing costs soared on the back of a jump in oil and gas prices after the latest US and Iran attacks on ships in the strait of Hormuz.

The interest rate, or yield, on UK government debt rose to a 19-year high on Thursday, while the yield on US and European bonds also climbed in line with oil, which touched $105 (£78) a barrel.

Investors had expected the ECB to raise the cost of borrowing across the euro bloc, but were spooked by the hawkish tone of the central bank’s report, which warned of inflationary pressures building in many sectors of the economy.

Increasing its main rate from 2.25% to the highest level since March last year, the central bank lifted its forecast for eurozone economic growth in 2026 to 0.9%, up from 0.8% in June. It now expects inflation to average 3% this year.

The biggest driving force of rising prices is the cost of energy, which again jumped on Thursday after this week’s increase in US and Iranian attacks on ships transiting the Gulf.

Brent crude passed $105 a barrel, before slipping back to about $104.5, a 3.3% rise on the day. British gas prices rose to above 203p per therm, the highest since December 2022.

Continental European gas prices also increased. The Dutch wholesale gas price – the EU standard – passed €80 per megawatt hour (MWh) for the first time since January 2023. The front-month contract is trading 3.4% higher at €82.56/MWh.

This, in turn, increased government borrowing costs in leading economies. The interest rate on benchmark 10-year UK government bonds, also known as gilts, hit 5.36%, the highest since August 2007.

The rate on Germany’s 30-year government bond rose 2.5 basis points to 5.08%, the highest since December 2003. The 10-year yield hit 3.45%, the highest since April 2011. France’s 10-year government bond yield was the highest since October 2008 at 4.344%, up 1 basis point.

Central banks are concerned that high fuel and energy prices will feed into higher transport costs and more expensive heating for commercial and residential properties, which will lead to a broad-based rise in inflation.

The ECB president, Christine Lagarde, said: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated,” adding that food inflation, which had remained low at 1.2%, was likely to increase in response to higher oil and gas prices.

She explicitly acknowledged ‌that gas prices could rise owing to further supply disruptions or an unusually cold winter in combination with low storage levels across much of the region.

Investors are concerned that UK and EU governments have underplayed the risk of running out of gas and the negative effect a subsequent dash for supplies will have on inflation. Recent data shows EU gas stores are only 67% full, well below the five-year average of 84%.

UK and continental European gas buyers have delayed filling gas stores in the expectation that the Middle East conflict will be resolved and prices will be lower before winter in the northern hemisphere. As the war drags on, there is the prospect of gas prices rising because of a scramble of buyers looking to replenish stocks before cold weather arrives.

Bond markets were also put on alert by the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, who said the US would buy back $6bn worth of government debt – known as US treasuries – in an effort to alleviate a sell-off in the US bond market that has put pressure on interest rates.

But the size of the package was considered inadequate by bond buyers and the yield on 10-year treasuries rose to a three-year high.

“Headline inflation is expected to return to around target towards the end of 2027, supported by the effects of higher interest rates,” Lagarde said.

Asked about the ECB’s next move, she said: “We have not debated at all any kind of future path. Markets do what they have to do and we do what ​we have to do – which is to provide price stability.”

Business.title: Apple’s new CEO introduces himself at annual showcase: ‘I continue to be inspired every single day’
Business.text:
John Ternus, Apple’s new CEO, helmed the company’s annual showcase of new iPhones and other products on Wednesday. It was the first time the public saw the warm and unpretentious demeanor of the executive, who is filling the shoes of Tim Cook and his predecessor, Steve Jobs, at the $4.5tn tech giant.

The event kicked off with a video montage of characters describing the best way to start a movie, from a getaway scene to a closeup of woman revealing her true identity, before the well-known voice of Cook piped in.

“Camera follows a mysterious figure before revealing our main character,” Cook said. “No. Not me. That’s your guy. That’s your opener.”

The figure came into focus: Ternus.

“I want to take a moment to express what an extraordinary privilege it is to represent the remarkable teams here at Apple,” Ternus said. “I’ve spent much of my life at this company, and I continue to be inspired every single day by the curiosity, invention and relentless pursuit of excellence that define Apple.”

Not much is publicly known about Ternus’s leadership style, even though he has worked at Apple for 25 years. He has kept a low profile and is known for a calm manner and attention to detail. Ternus started at the company in 2001 and in 2013 became the vice-president of hardware engineering. By 2021, he was heading the entire hardware department.

In Apple tradition, Ternus, as the CEO, kicked off Wednesday’s keynote address and cued up the gadget reveals. Apple made big announcements at its “Surprise and Shine” event in Cupertino, California, including its first foldable phone, called iPhone Duo, as well as upgrades to standard iPhones, AirPods headphones and Apple Watch lines.

Ternus hosted the event in a friendly style, presenting himself in everyman attire of a dark, crew-neck maroon sweater and black jeans. Nearly an hour after the event started, he began to tease the announcement of iPhone Duo, saying: “Actually, there is one more thing …”

Then, taking the phone from the back pocket of his jeans and holding it up to the camera, he said with a coy smile, “this is iPhone Duo.”

Ternus cast the Duo, with its wider displays and multidirectional cameras, as an upgrade to the iPhone experience, rather than the technological revolution Jobs described when he unveiled the original iPhone in 2007.

He said the Duo “will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone”.

Bob O’Donnell, the president and chief analyst of Technalysis Research, said: “While products like the expected foldable iPhone have been in the works for some time, the fact that, as the new CEO, John Ternus gets to introduce it to the world is hugely symbolic because it shows off how a new era of more interesting new products for the company is kicking off under his leadership.”

Jobs, Apple’s greatest showman, was known for his commanding stage presence, donning his black turtleneck and blue jeans uniform. When he debuted the first iPhone, he paced back and forth on the stage, drumming up suspense, then said: “Every once in a while, a revolutionary product comes along that changes everything.” The crowd went wild.

Cook had a much calmer demeanor, often holding his hands as if clasped in prayer and repeating a similar mantra during Apple’s iPhone events: “We think you’re gonna love it” and “This is the best iPhone we’ve ever created.”

Under Cook, Apple became a hardware juggernaut, and he turned the company into the world’s first trillion-dollar business. Although he was not considered a visionary like Jobs, Cook was credited with the pragmatism that made Apple a lucrative success.

When the company announced in April that Ternus was taking over from Cook, Ternus said he was “profoundly grateful” to “carry Apple’s mission forward”.

“I have been lucky to have worked under Steve Jobs and to have had Tim Cook as my mentor,” he added. “I am humbled to step into this role.”

Cook praised his successor as having “the mind of an engineer, the soul of an innovator and the heart to lead with integrity and with honor”.

Dipanjan Chatterjee, a principal analyst at Forrester, said that Ternus inheriting this legacy would be “both a boon and a burden for him”. The new CEO would need to continue with Cook’s scale and monetization, he said, while also moving toward the future with new advancements in technology other than smartphones.

“His first keynote will set the tone for his vision of Apple’s future,” Chatterjee said.

Sports.title: Hull City's Sorba Thomas crashes outside training ground
Sports.text:
Premier League winger Sorba Thomas has been involved in a car crash close to Hull City's training ground, the club has confirmed.

The 27-year-old walked away from the crash, which happened on Millhouse Woods Lane in Cottingham on Friday morning. His vehicle, a grey Land Rover Defender, was pictured on its roof, with broken windows.

Humberside Police said emergency services remained at the scene and asked people to avoid the area.

In a statement, the club said it was "relieved" to hear its player, who joined the Tigers from Championship side Stoke City earlier this month, was unharmed.

The club added: "The club is aware of images of Sorba's car circulating on social media and can reassure supporters that he has sustained no injuries and emerged from his vehicle completely unscathed."

A woman who lives at the scene said the crash, which happened at about 08:30 BST, woke her up.

"I was laid in bed [and] heard a noise – crash, bang," she said.

"I got up, come down and the car is in my hedge."

An NHS worker who lives on the road said the incident had left him unable to go to work as the road was blocked.

"There will be patients who will miss appointments because of this," he said.

"It's one road in and one road out. It was an accident waiting to happen."

Sports.title: Hull City fined £30k by FA & bans issued over discriminatory chants
Sports.text:
Hull City have been fined £30,000 over discriminatory chanting during their 4-0 FA Cup defeat by Chelsea in February.

The club is now urging supporters not to engage in the same chant when they face the Blues in the Premier League on Saturday.

And it revealed three supporters had been banned for "a minimum of three years" following February's game at the MKM Stadium.

Three people were arrested for allegedly engaging in homophobic chanting at the match, in which spectators were repeatedly warned to stop the chants over the PA system and messages were displayed on screens.

The chanting was condemned by one fan group as a "stain on our game".

The Football Association later charged the club with failing "to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters) do not use words or behave in an improper, offensive, abusive, indecent or insulting way with a reference - whether express or implied - to sexual orientation" and on Friday announced the club had accepted the charge and received a £30,000 fine.

"Hull City condemns, in the strongest possible terms, the offensive and inappropriate language used by the supporters responsible," the club said, saying the "chant in question is recognised as a homophobic slur and its use may constitute a hate crime".

It warned those using the chant faced arrest and criminal charges.

"Ahead of Saturday's trip to Stamford Bridge, the club reminds all supporters that discrimination of any kind is wholly unacceptable and will not be tolerated," it added.

Sports.title: US Open 2026 semi-finals: Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton look to bounce back from late-night finishes
Sports.text:
New York is known as the city that never sleeps - and so it has been at this year's US Open.

A number of matches have started late and finished in the early hours, backing up the city's reputation as a playground for the nocturnal.

But when some players - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev - are heading to bed as Manhattan commuters are waking up for work, it raises questions about fairness.

Three of top seed Zverev's five matches over the past fortnight have finished past 1am.

"I've been to bed as late as 6:45am in the past week so I'm kind of a bit jet-lagged," Zverev said.

"I feel like I'm playing the Australian Open in New York right now."

Friday's semi-final against Karen Khachanov - not before 15:00 local time/20:00 BST - will be the first time the German has played in the day at this year's US Open.

By contrast, unseeded Khachanov has not been on court beyond midnight. He also has slightly longer to prepare after his quarter-final against Alexander Blockx finished shortly before 19:00 local time on Wednesday.

American eighth seed Shelton did not complete his last-eight victory over Carlos Alcaraz until 3:34am on Wednesday.

Shelton faces 11th seed Frances Tiafoe, who wrapped up his quarter-final about 19:00 on Tuesday after beating US compatriot Alex Michelsen in a five-set epic.

"The advantage of the opponent who has played earlier in the day will be big - they've had that full evening's rest and a good night's sleep," Matt Little, who was Andy Murray's long-time strength and conditioning coach, told BBC Sport.

"We can all relate to it - if you have one really bad night's sleep, you have the knock-on effect of that for the coming days."

Little saw the effects first hand when Murray infamously finished a match at 4am at the 2023 Australian Open, with the former world number one managing only three hours sleep before returning to Melbourne Park about 11am the following day.

Zverev did not go to bed until gone 5am following his opening three victories at Flushing Meadows and stayed up to watch Shelton beat Alcaraz on his night off.

Shelton, who meets Tiafoe in Friday's night session (19:00 local time/00:00 BST, Sat), insisted he would pull up "all right" after two days off court.

"He'll have to be napping to catch up some sleep," said Little.

"On the nutritional side, he'll be making sure he gets as many carbs and as much protein as he can in for that next match, and trying to get back to a bit of a routine.

"It's about making sure you can optimise the hydration and get as much sleep as possible without completely going into a full slumber."

Murray described the situation in Melbourne - where he beat Thanasi Kokkinakis in the second-latest finish in Grand Slam history - as a "farce".

Few disagreed, and slight tweaks have been made in an attempt to limit matches finishing at the crack of dawn.

In response to Murray's match, the Australian Open cut the number of day-session matches on the main courts from three to two to reduce the risk of night sessions being delayed.

In early 2024, the ATP and WTA created new rules which prevented tour matches - played over three sets and not five like the Slams - starting after 23:00. These rules, however, do not apply at the majors.

A number of matches have started late and finished in the early hours, backing up the city's reputation as a playground for the nocturnal. Sports.title: Celtic: Boss Martin O'Neill says side given 'timely' police reminder before derby
Sports.text:
Manager Martin O'Neill says Celtic had a visit from Police Scotland on Friday to give them "a timely reminder" about their "general behaviour" in Sunday's Premier Sport Cup quarter-final against city rivals Rangers.

Both Glasgow clubs were last month ordered to play their next home Scottish Cup matches behind closed doors after last season's quarter-final - won by Celtic after a penalty shootout at Ibrox - was marred by fan disorder.

It will be the first time Celtic have returned there since, although the Scottish champions did host a Scottish Premiership encounter in May, beating Rangers 3-1.

The Scottish Professional Football League recently announced no away fans will attend Old Firm derbies in the league or League Cup this season.

"We had the police come in today, just a little 15-minute meeting to remind us of our behaviour, which I think is a timely reminder," O'Neill revealed.

Asked what had been said, the Northern Irishman said: "They didn't mention this, but I would have assumed that one of the things that would be considered is what happens in the field of play, because these things can be taken further.

"You don't want any sort of punch-ups for a start. Secondly, you don't want excessive celebrations, stuff like that.

"But I think it's just the behaviour in the light of what has happened in recent fixtures. I think that the conversation with the police wouldn't have taken place had not recent events been brought up to us."

Celtic have won the latest three derbies since Rangers beat them 3-1 at Celtic Park in the league in January - and are five points ahead in the Premiership after just six games of the new season.

Asked how having no away fans might impact the match, O'Neill added: "I think the games themselves almost take care of themselves in that sense.

"It'll be strange in many aspects not to have any away fans in our area. I always felt as if it would give you a crumb of comfort in some description.

"Nervously looking forward to it, excitedly looking forward to it."

Rangers have come in for some criticism from their own fans for a poor start to the season under new manager Derek McInnes, although the hosts are on a run of four successive victories.

"I suppose if you get in front in the game, that makes them anxious," O'Neill suggested.

"Talking about getting in front and getting in front are two different things. The crowd will be right behind their team, which you would expect.

"We just do our best. We know that we're up against a very fine side. We're up against a crowd that can make a difference. I'd be delighted to be celebrating something in the game."

Sports.title: Newcastle: Lewis Hall signs new contract until 2031
Sports.text:
Newcastle United defender Lewis Hall has signed a new contract with the club that runs until 2031.

The left-back, who has been the subject of interest from Manchester United, has agreed a two-year extension to his original deal.

Hall said it was a "really proud moment" to extend his stay as a boyhood supporter of the club.

"It's an absolute pleasure to play for this club and to represent the supporters," he said. "I know how much it means to them.

"To be able to bring joy to their faces, it's a big thing for me. I obviously have a family connection with the club, which is incredibly important to us all.

"One of the main reasons I play is to make my family proud, and I know how much it means to them to watch me playing for Newcastle United.

"It's a really good place to be. It's really pleasing with how we've started the season, especially with the new gaffer [Matthias Jaissle] and coaching staff coming in, and I think we can go on to achieve really big things."

Hall, 22, has made 106 appearances for Newcastle since joining the club from Chelsea in 2023.

Jaissle said the defender is a "very important player for us and for what we are building here".

"His mentality is exactly what you want in a young player," he said. "He wants to learn every day and he wants to be better in every match.

"Lewis covers ground in a way that few players can. He defends with maturity and intelligence, and his technical level means he can support the team higher up the pitch.

"What excites me most is that I believe the best is still to come from Lewis. He has a lot of room to develop, and I am looking forward to working with him as he grows with us."

Sports.title: Premier League predictions: Chris Sutton v Dorking Wanderers manager Marc White - & AI
Sports.text:
New Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca has made a table-topping start, but will his 100% Premier League record survive Sunday's short trip to Old Trafford?

"Marcus Rashford is fit and has looked a threat when I've seen him play," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton. "Because of that, I can see Manchester United scoring.

"But United have conceded twice against Hull, Ipswich and Everton, so why wouldn't they ship goals against City too?"

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week four, he takes on Dorking Wanderers manager Marc White.

White's story as founder, player and manager of his own club was the subject of a docuseries,, external which racked up more than half a billion views by the end of 2025. You can also follow his strategies and insights on TikTok., external

Do you agree with Sutton and White's scores? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions.

Seeing his club win a place in the Football League remains the aim for White, but reaching the Premier League feels a far more distant dream.

"For me the gulf in football is between the Premier League and some Championship clubs, and the rest," White told BBC Sport.

"The Premier League is still the elite place to be, and it's like being part of a financial institution when you are there, but you need to spend your money wisely.

"One big theory I have, if you flip it around the other way, is you would not want to get relegated from the Premier League.

"There are clubs in there, like Fulham or Bournemouth and Brentford, where arguably there are much bigger clubs than them in the Championship.

"That next manager is always so important for clubs of that size because, if they get it wrong and go down, some of them may never come back.

"The Championship is a little bit divided too. We do a lot of business with Charlton Athletic, and their finances, compared to the majority of that division, are nothing. There's no comparison between them and West Ham, for example. They are miles apart.

"Beyond that, there is not such a gap, but you can definitely put a thick border between the Championship and League One.

"I think that's why you see the likes of Bromley and Stockport go on the same journey from non-league that we are trying to make, and go up from League Two too. But then they get to League One and it is like the next bit is the tough bit."

Chris Sutton and Marc White were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Villa Park, 15:00 BST

This is a hard one to start with because, while Aston Villa still haven't won or scored in the Premier League, they got a good win over Club Brugge in the Champions League on Tuesday.

Nicolas Jackson got off the mark in that game and, although his finishing can be erratic, he's the kind of player who will mature and get better every season. I think he will do well for them.

Forest are also yet to win. I know there was controversy over Neco Williams' disallowed goal in their draw against Spurs last time out but I do think they got the decision right in the end.

This is going to be close and I am tempted to go for another Forest draw, but Villa are obviously going to score in the Premier League at some point so I'll be brave and say they will edge it.

Sutton's prediction: 2-1

Marc's prediction: Villa have been turned inside-out over the summer, but they fall into that category of having a great manager and Unai Emery will stabilise them. 1-1

AI's prediction: 2-1

Vitality Stadium, 15:00

To say Bournemouth keep on throwing it away is a bit harsh, but they have been ahead in all three of their league games so far and have not won any of them.

Will they see this one through? I am not sure, but I like the way Cherries boss Marco Rose talks when he has been interviewed after games. He is a bright guy and he will get things right.

I was spot on with my prediction for Brentford's 1-1 draw with Sunderland last week, but the Bees were actually lucky to get a point in the end.

Brentford will play on the counter-attack here and Bournemouth will have a go at them, so this smells like a draw to me.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

Marc's prediction: It's mad to think this was a League Two fixture in 2009, when Bournemouth almost went out of the Football League. With Brentford, it could be just a matter of time before Keith Andrews is seen as a manager who is desired by the big clubs. If he has another good season, someone will be in for him. 1-2

AI's prediction: 2-2

Stamford Bridge, 15:00

I have happy memories of this fixture because one of my three goals for Chelsea came against Hull, in the FA Cup.

Hull haven't conceded yet and they are the team I have been most wrong about so far this season.

With every passing week, they are putting more egg on my face [see the table based on Sutton's predictions at the bottom of the page] but it can't keep happening, can it?

It probably can, but I am still going for Chelsea to win this. The Tigers have defended brilliantly so far, but they are not going to keep out Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro.

Hull will defend ferociously but, as Chelsea showed in the Carabao Cup against Leeds on Wednesday, they have enough quality to play through teams who sit in; and, if they score first, then Hull will have to open up - that's my theory anyway.

The only thing I was unsure about was whether Hull would score too. Chelsea still seem to be a bit chaotic with the way they defend, and they have leaked a few goals, but I have given them a clean sheet. They need one.

Sutton's prediction: 3-0

Marc's prediction: It's a bit like Beauty and the Beast, this. Hull will be quite happy to be the beast, but there are some games where that won't work. With Chelsea's front-line, this is one of them. 4-0

AI's prediction: 3-0

Selhurst Park, 15:00

Crystal Palace picked up their first win under Pierre Sage last weekend, which was really important for them.

They have still got goals in their team, as they showed against Fulham, but it was quite an open game and they always look like they will concede a few too.

I covered Ipswich's defeat by Liverpool and what worries me a little bit is the way their manager Gary O'Neil saw that game.

He was overly positive about his team's performance and, while I know why he is doing it, you can't mask that they didn't match Liverpool and they were not creative enough in the final third either - I don't remember Alisson having to make a save of note.

This feels like an important game for Ipswich after two successive defeats but I don't know why I am thinking they will get a point because that's not going to happen, is it?

My first thought was that they will grind out a draw, but I've changed my mind and am going with Palace to take the points at home.

Sutton's prediction: 2-1

Marc's prediction: Palace are in the bracket of clubs who might be in trouble this year, but I have put this down as a draw because they have got that Selhurst Park thing going on. 1-1

AI's prediction: 2-0

I am covering this game for 5 Live and will be co-commentating with Ian Dennis.

For Fulham, the big talking point is their manager, and whether they will sink any lower under Alvaro Arbeloa. He will be under pressure until he gets his first Premier League win.

Fulham look a little bit lightweight to me and, while Cesar Palacios in midfield and Gonzalo Garcia up front have clearly got something about them, it is always going to be hard for any young player to hit the ground running when they are thrown into the Premier League, especially under a manager who is new too.

If you don't get off to a good start, you are going to be scrutinised. It is the same for every manager and, while Fulham have got some good attacking players, they are shipping goals at the other end.

To lead twice against Palace, who had also started the season poorly, and still lose makes this game even bigger for Arbeloa.

He is trying to play a high pressing game, and he also wants to dominate the ball, but at the highest level, which the Premier League is, if you are not on point with your press then teams will play through you.

Arbeloa needs a result to kickstart his season, or at least something to grab hold of, and I don't think it's impossible for them to get something at Anfield.

I certainly don't think Liverpool have cracked it after watching them win at Ipswich, and they will give up some chances with their high defensive line too.

Fulham will score, but the problem for Arbeloa is that Liverpool will score more.

Sutton's prediction: 2-1

Marc on why he follows Fulham: I went to watch Fulham as a really small kid, which was my first memory of 'big' football, standing on the terrace at Craven Cottage, and I still go there now whenever we're not playing. I am friends with the captain, Tom Cairney, so luckily I get to watch them quite a lot. They are quite a unique family club at that level and I really enjoy it, plus it's a good chance to watch Premier League football.

Marc's prediction: Fulham have done the opposite of what Brentford did when Thomas Frank left. They don't just have a new manager to replace Marco Silva, they have a new system and with new players. It's a big gamble. 3-1

AI's prediction: 3-1

Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, 17:30

This is absolutely massive for Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi. First and foremost, though, he needs to take a bit of responsibility for his side's poor results.

He blamed the Spurs strikers after their 0-0 draw with Nottingham Forest, but at least he has got some in his squad.

I just find it wild that in a billion-dollar industry, which football is now, Everton got themselves in a position where they let Beto leave, knowing there was a possibility that Folarin Balogun might fail his medical and without having anyone else lined up.

Could they still go to Spurs and nick something? Absolutely. I am still not sure whether Tottenham being at home counts as an advantage.

But this game has a draw written all over it, and is actually an easy game to predict.

Spurs are a 'law of averages' team, or at least that's the way I see it. Eventually they have to score and eventually they have to win too, but I don't see both things happening this weekend.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

Marc's prediction: Spurs have a new team but continue to frustrate their fans, while Everton just seem to go about their business. 2-2

AI's prediction: 2-1

Stadium of Light, 20:00

This was a cracking game last season, which finished 2-2, and is arguably Arsenal's toughest test so far in this campaign.

I really like Sunderland and their European campaign has not started yet so those extra games won't affect them here.

I feel like being brave and giving them a draw because they are well capable of taking a point off Arsenal, but the Gunners just have the ability to shut up shop when they need to, and they can get physical again if they need to.

Thinking about it, I can't really go against an Arsenal victory, because of the players they were able to bring on in last weekend's comeback win against Chelsea.

They have got A-list replacements everywhere they look and, if they need a goal against Sunderland, I can see them bringing someone on to get them one.

Sutton's prediction: 0-1

Marc's prediction: I'm a bit worried about Sunderland this season. They had a lot of momentum last year, and they also made a really good start. 1-3

AI's prediction: 1-3

Old Trafford, 16:30

I have got this result really badly wrong over the past couple of seasons, when I have tended to go for City, but I am not sure this time.

City are more methodical under Enzo Maresca, with the way that he builds play from the back - they won't be swashbuckling, put it that way.

I don't think he has changed much about his way of playing from when he was in charge at Chelsea, and United will be ready for that.

I really like United boss Michael Carrick and the way he does not get too carried away, win or lose.

Everton's late equaliser would have felt like a loss last weekend, but United still haven't clicked in attack yet, and that's part of the problem for them.

Then I look at the goals they are shipping too, and wonder if they are really good enough to keep City out?

I am not so sure they are, but I also think they can hurt City.

City have made a brilliant start, with four wins out of four in all competitions since the Premier League got under way, but if they looked a little vulnerable against Coventry then United are going to cause them more problems.

Sutton's prediction: 2-2

Marc's prediction: I think I know the way this is going for United. Carrick has had that natural bounce that a former player is going to get but, long term, sustaining that is tough. For me, he could become a manager under pressure this year.

With City, it's a sign of a good manager for them to start like this under Maresca. I have them down as clear winners here. 0-2

AI's prediction: 2-2

Elland Road, 20:00

Newcastle are the new counter-attack kings and I am expecting more of the same from them here.

It will be interesting to see how Leeds boss Daniel Farke tries to deal with that. He has been quite versatile with the way he has set his side up this season.

Leeds have shown a bit more steel in their league games too, and look well organised, but at the same time I don't know if they carry as much of an attacking threat as they did previously.

I probably still fancy Leeds more to win this because they are at home, but Newcastle showed plenty of fight against Bournemouth last week and this will probably end up in a draw too.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

Marc's prediction: A Monday night thriller. 2-3

AI's prediction: 1-2

As Chris said after a successful week two, "it's not how you start the weekend, it's how you finish it".

It was the final few fixtures which decided the outcome this time too - only it wasn't Chris who took the victory in week three.

He was leading on Saturday night after eight of the weekend's 10 games had been played, but his guest, Kasabian frontman Serge Pizzorno, enjoyed a 'Super Sunday' with exact scores in both remaining games to snatch the overall win.

Chris ended up with six correct results, including one exact score, for a total of 90 points.

That was enough to beat the BBC readers, who managed four correct results with one exact score for a tally of 70 points, and also AI, which got three correct results and one exact score, giving it 60 points.

It was Serge who surged to victory, however, after correctly predicting Everton's 2-2 draw with Manchester United and Arsenal's 2-1 win over Chelsea.

He got four correct results but those two exact scores proved decisive, giving him a winning total of 100 points.

Everyone was right about only two of the fixtures - Liverpool's win at Ipswich and Manchester City's victory over Coventry.

There were three fixtures where none of our predictors picked the right outcome - the draws in Newcastle-Bournemouth and Brighton-Leeds, and Crystal Palace's 3-2 win at Fulham.

From more than 37,000 predictions, only around 5,000 (14%) went for any sort of Palace win, and only 79 of you got the correct scoreline.

Sports.title: Garcia vs Benn: 'He lives through me' - why Nigel Benn can't walk away from Conor
Sports.text:
Nigel Benn had insisted he was stepping away from his son's career for good.

The 10,000-mile trips from Australia - where Nigel is based - were done, and Conor Benn was on his own after his grudge-match win over Chris Eubank Jr.

Yet in the build-up to Conor's WBC welterweight world title challenge against Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas, the 'Dark Destroyer' was by his son's side at the news conference and holding court at their Essex media day - as embedded as ever.

Ask Nigel why and he claims Conor "twisted my arm" into helping with one final hurdle.

"I don't know if he was lying or if he believed it himself," Conor says with a wry smile.

"He lives through me. He goes, 'son, this is my last fight, I'm done.' Then the next one it's, 'son, it's your first defence.' There'll always be something."

Perhaps neither man is ready to cut the cord.

Conor has stepped out of his 62-year-old father's shadow - not by matching the legendary ring achievements, but through the sheer turbulence of his own journey.

Navigating a career-threatening doping case, surviving the ferocious Eubank rivalry and acrimoniously splitting from long-time promoter Eddie Hearn transformed him from 'Nigel's boy' into one of British boxing's most polarising headliners.

Through those storms, Nigel has been there in the trenches.

"It's what Conor thinks and what his dad thinks - that's what it's about, not what everybody else says," Nigel Benn says.

"Everyone's not going to love my son. Everybody didn't love me. But once you get that belt around his waist, we'll go from there."

Thirty-six years ago, Nigel flew across the Atlantic as the fiery outsider, tearing through Doug DeWitt in Atlantic City to secure his first world title.

Now, Conor lands on the Las Vegas Strip chasing the exact same milestone. A victory would place the Benns alongside the likes of Floyd and Tracy Harris Patterson, Julio Cesar Chavez and Julio Cesar Chavez Jr and Leon and Cory Spinks in the lineage of father-and-son world champions.

"I've watched him religiously for 10 years put his life on the line," Nigel says. "He's just going from strength to strength, from glory to glory. I see him being victorious. I'm not actually worried whatsoever."

Yet reaching this point has required navigating a volatile road fraught with controversy.

The adverse drug test findings that wiped out two years of Conor's career cast a long shadow, fracturing public perception and leaving unanswered questions that still follow him.

He has always denied doping, a provisional suspension was lifted in November 2024, and he says he has fought throughout his career as "an advocate for clean sport".

Inside the ropes, the jury remains stubbornly out on his talent.

A laboured points victory over Regis Prograis in his last outing did little to convince purists he belongs at the sport's highest echelon.

But Conor cares little for the outside noise or winning over the boxing fraternity.

"To some people, I'll never be good enough," he says. "One day they love you, some day they hate you.

"You keep talking about what other people think, but I don't care. Winning the world title for me, it's personal. If I listen to other people, I wouldn't be where I am."

Garcia has walked an equally chaotic path, having served a one-year suspension after testing positive for banned substance ostarine following his win over Devin Haney in 2024.

Both men deny intentionally ever taking performance-enhancing drugs, but away from that issue their showdown is wrapped in the contradictions that define modern boxing.

It will be staged by UFC-backed Zuffa Boxing - following Conor's high-profile split from Hearn - yet featuring the traditional green-and-gold WBC belt on the line, despite Zuffa's public rhetoric about disrupting boxing's old-guard sanctioning bodies.

Social media spats between the fighters have brought plenty of heat, but Conor Benn does not compare it to the raw nature of the Eubank saga, which spilled over into face-to-face fury. An egg was even slapped across Benn's face by Eubank.

"Listen, it's not personal with Ryan. It is personal with Eubank - this ain't no comparison," Conor says.

"One person I wanted to put in hospital; the other one I don't. I just want his title and I want his number one position. I've been at world level for years and for me to claim the number one spot officially is the goal here.

"[Garcia] is like a child. It doesn't bother me. You need people like Ryan in the sport of boxing."

Garcia is proven at the top level and enters as the favourite, bringing blinding hand speed and a fight-ending left hook.

But Nigel Benn believes he has mapped out the exact antidote to Garcia's firepower. He says his son should attack Garcia using suffocating, bobbing aggression - the kind that Nigel used to blow out Iran Barkley in 1990.

"When he goes under pressure, what happens? He falls and his heart doesn't go into it," Nigel says.

"For the first time, [Conor] is actually sitting there listening. He has to be not the destroyer, he has to be the Dark Destroyer. Controlled aggression.

"Don't give him room. Roll under his punches, left hook to the body, left hook to the head. He knows what to do."

The hostile Vegas spotlight, meanwhile, evokes memories of Benn senior's ferocious 1995 battle with Gerald McClellan.

"Everybody had me to be blown out within round three. Exactly the same thing as what they do with Conor," Nigel says. "And I know he's going to prevail."

Win, lose or draw, Nigel insists this time he will walk away for good and let Conor do his own thing.

"I can walk out of that arena, go home, and be with my family, and that's it," Nigel says.

Whether Nigel finally catches that one-way flight back to Sydney is another matter.

If Conor leaves Las Vegas with the WBC belt around his waist, you would not bet against his father being back for defence number one.

Sports.title: Five-set tennis is under attack. Killing it would be a colossal unforced error
Sports.text:
Tuesday night’s quarter-final match between Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz had everything a US Open spectacle could ask for: huge stakes, knife-edge drama, top-shelf competition and an American hero who comes through in the end. The only fault to find was really the matter of time. The first ball wasn’t struck until 11.05 in the evening, and Shelton’s clinching ace didn’t come until 3.33 in the morning – marking, after a total of 4hr 28min on court, the latest-ending US Open match by a whopping 43 minutes.

Somewhat predictably, the discourse among media and fans following the late-night match has swiftly moved on from the USTA’s misadventures in scheduling to a referendum on the five-set match and whether it should be put out to pasture. For the record: that would be a colossal unforced error.

Five-setters aren’t just intrinsic to the grand slam canon. They are a badge of honor in the men’s game, confirmation that a player can and did indeed hack it in the big leagues. John Isner may not have won a major during his time on tour. But his capacity for grinding out marathon matches – not least the three-day, 11-hour epic he played against Nicholas Mahut at Wimbledon in 2010 – is why he remains highly respected by peers and fans alike.

Best-of-five is the exclusive framing device for the best matches in history and an imprimatur of the sport’s most revered champions. (See, The Greatest Match Ever Played or last year’s French Open final.) Even the losers are celebrated merely for having survived and played on to become part of the tale. “People still remember this match but he didn’t know if I was the winner,” Mahut said in 2015. “So, maybe, in 10 years people will think I won the match.”

Five-setters are the mother of sporting crucibles – a test of will, nerve and focus. That holds true as much for the men who play as their spectators. Much of what makes the experience of following tennis so affirming is the global group-watch sessions that take over social media anytime an Australian Open match goes the distance.

Viewers who can’t babysit the full marathon into the night – lest they risk sleeping through their morning alarms or, worse, cheering the exciting points too boisterously and rousing their house and neighbors – get to wake up and find the fifth set still raging as they’re getting ready for work the next day. A skeptic might point to the Australian Open, perhaps more so than any other slam, as a prime reason to abolish the five-setter. But true tennis nerds see the Happy Slam for what it is: a rite of passage. In fact, if they don’t seem surprised by the US Open’s Melbourne hours, it’s because Craig Tiley, formerly the CEO of Tennis Australia, is now running the USTA.

Still, for all the honor and valor there is to be extracted from five-setters, especially as they pile up, there’s no denying the matches exact a physical toll from players that has become harder to ignore as the pressure to maintain a hectic touring calendar puts them at increasing risk of missing tournaments from wear and tear. That tension between tradition and evolution has animated an existential debate around five-setters that has been simmering for years.

Last month, incoming Tennis Australia CEO Andrew Abdo tossed out ideas for a shorter-form game. “Maybe we’re not playing best of five all the way through,” Abdo said at a Melbourne sports conference. “Maybe the point scoring system changes. Maybe there are different permutations to how we engage and entertain audiences without losing the fabric, and what really makes the sport special.”

Abdo’s remarks – which come after Tiley, his predecessor, suggested women play five-set matches – might not have resonated if Novak Djokovic, the slam king who built his reputation on five-set matches, hadn’t first proposed changes to the scoring system that would keep the five sets but dilute the number of games to “keep the matches within a two-hour window”. And even though the 24-time major champion was being somewhat facetious – he was specifically asked for an opinion that would inflame fans – it didn’t stop John McEnroe, tennis’ self-righteous conscience, from breaking out his gas canister. “People’s attention spans are shorter than ever,” said McEnroe – famously, the five-set loser of an epic 1980 Wimbledon final canonized as the War of 18-16.

But those voices, however prominent, have yet to reach a volume that drowns out five-set traditionalists. “Do I love five setters? Absolutely not,” Frances Tiafoe said after hanging on to beat fellow American Alex Michelsen in a five-set quarterfinal he surely would’ve lost if the scoring revolutionists had their way. “When I’m up two sets to love I would love to shake hands and go home. But it’s tennis, man. I grew up watching incredible tennis, incredible five setters. Novak vs Rafa, Federer vs Rafa. Incredible five setters which go on for hours and hours. That is the history of the game.”

The quarter-final between Shelton and Alcaraz wrote another chapter, one that gave Arthur Ashe Stadium the feel of a Queens dive after last call. Shelton, still woozy from outlasting the US Open’s defending champion, beseeched his sister’s employer, Morgan Stanley, to give her the day off from work. (She was due back by 6am.) As he and Alcaraz contested the final points, with Tuesday having turned into Wednesday, custodial workers could be seen and heard tidying up the stadium and grounds for the horde to come after sunrise. On social media, US Open patrons who hung on til the bitter end shared the outrageous surge pricing they encountered for rideshares back home (“I could get a hotel, bro”) and posted videos of exhausted ballkids hustling back into the city before school starts “in three hours”.

No one’s suggesting the US Open needs a curfew. (That’s Wimbledon’s turf, after all.) There’s a simple fix to the late-night match problem that doesn’t involve fundamentally restructuring the way the men’s game is played. The USTA could just move one of its primetime features to the world’s 13th-largest tennis show court – Louis Armstrong Stadium, right next door to Ashe – and move the start times up to ensure play didn’t extend much past midnight. The start of Shelton-Alcaraz was delayed by Jessica Pegula and Emma Navarro taking three sets to wrap up their quarter-final, which was itself delayed by the afternoon matches ahead of them going long. But that might mean missing out on the filthy lucre that Ashe generates from its doubled capacity and extravagant suites – and god forbid the USTA make slightly less money.

The funny thing about all this panting to change tennis for its own good is that tennis has changed so much already. Electronic line calls, 10-point tiebreaks, on-court coaching, the serve clock – the hidebound sport has proven it can be tweaked for pace and entertainment without a cost to its core integrity.

But what truly makes the talk about abolishing the five-setter so hard to hear, particularly from veterans of those wars, is the fundamental misunderstanding. In other sports, time has a negative correlation. Who among us hasn’t been held hostage by the football game that lumbers on because the coach can’t be bothered to take their timeouts home? Who among us hasn’t been prisoner to a basketball game that would have ended in 30 seconds if it hadn’t been for all the fouling?

In tennis, a match that stretches on for hours and hours isn’t a drag. It’s an obvious marker of quality, an implied reason to tune in. And if engagement is the name of the game, the drama of a fifth act that holds the potential to maintain an audience, capture a new one and – in the case of the Shelton-Alcaraz quarter – extend the primetime viewing window on the West Coast – should be an incentive for those committed to growing the game to embrace the five-setter even tighter, not abolish it.

One can just imagine the lines that would be drawn if the five-set format ever changed: the players who come after having to put up with cranky veterans of those five-set marathons of yesteryear prattling on about how the real legends were forged in my day. That’s no kind of ending for a sport that has a great ending already.

The only fault to find was really the matter of time. The first ball wasn’t struck...

Sports.title: Crowd of 100,000 laps up relentless sensory experience as NFL woos Melbourne
Sports.text:
At 9am on a Friday, Melbourne’s tongues would usually be tinged with toothpaste. Beer, however, was the flavour craved by this throng of bros brought together by the visit of one of the United States’ great institutions.

Dressed in San Francisco 49ers red, LA Rams blue and every other colour of the 32-team NFL rainbow, the 100,021 fans had come to the competition’s first regular season match in Australia. They were there in droves, and 90 minutes from kick-off their thirst had already forced the closure of the pop-up pub adjacent to the MCG.

The horde had paid hundreds of dollars, some even thousands, for the privilege of seeing athletes in the storied American pastime run out into Melbourne’s sporting cathedral. They had come from more than 30 countries, with almost one in 10 making the trip from the US. They had waited patiently in snaking lines that peaked around 7.30am, but even then it took only 20 minutes to get past security.

These Americophiles had spent years following the sport through ESPN and the Madden series of video games, via US podcasters and fantasy football. Here they were now, living their American sporting dream, celebrating a passion that had survived in the shadows of the Australian mainstream.

It is a hobby that reflects a reverence for the nation across the Pacific, one that is based on defensive lines, rather than defence bases. Aukus, in this context, appeared a natural fit.

One man, holding four large beers, was one of few in the crowd wearing a Jacksonville Jaguars jersey, even if he admitted he was a San Diego Chargers fan. His spirits were high, and sentiment genuine, when saying the vibes were “incredible”.

“I took the train here this morning and the amount of jerseys I saw was crazy,” he said, saying his name was Jarrod Wilson, who also happens to be a former Jaguars player. Alongside him was John Stockton, coincidentally one of the NBA’s greatest point guards. “We’ve counted every team jersey that we’ve seen and we’ve hit all 32,” Wilson said.

Apart from the cornucopia of licensed merchandise, the MCG turnout was clearly different to those that attend AFL and cricket games, the traditional sporting attractions in this corner of the country. There were very few children – it was a school day after all – and if there were roughly 10,000 Americans in the crowd, there appeared to be fewer women.

Alexandra Augustinus, who was there with her husband and brother and curious to see the spectacle first hand, was the only woman in her row. She said it felt “so different” to the AFL, but was impressed by an experience heavy on entertainment and a stadium full of enthusiasm. “I’ve been really shocked by how many Americans have come over, that’s really fun because they’re all dressed up, and they are massive fans. Everyone’s excited.”

In hotels, restaurants, pubs and retailers around Melbourne’s CBD, NAB predicted there would be $300m of economic activity this weekend. No one doubts this match has delivered an economic uplift – as well as showcasing Melbourne to millions of viewers overseas – but the bank would not clarify how much of that was over and above what would usually be spent. And the cost to host the match, reported to be at least $10m, is one borne by Victorian taxpayers.

Friday was the start of a four-year deal to have the NFL in Melbourne, although there may not be a match in Australia every season. The timing for next year already looks complicated given the start of the NFL season falls during the AFL finals. But few in attendance on Friday were concerned about next year.

Famous faces included AFL player Patrick Cripps and Jai Arrow, the NRL back rower forced into retirement due to motor neurone disease. Rugby league powerbroker Peter V’landys had also ventured into enemy territory, his own sport having gone the other way with their Las Vegas season opener.

A mellow US anthem before kick-off was appropriate for a match that marked 25 years since the September 11 terrorist attacks. That tragedy was acknowledged by the prominence of US Marines and the Australian Defence Force, who provided a fly-over. Advance Australia Fair was sung by pop star-slash-swimmer Cody Simpson, before Eddie McGuire and G-Flip came out to toss the coin as the boos – presumably for the former Collingwood president – rained down.

Organisers had imported the clear-bag policy, which barred patrons from bringing backpacks into the ground. Instead only small transparent plastic containers were allowed, roughly the size of an A4 piece of paper. It meant fans were expected to spend almost as long at the MCG as they might in a day of Test cricket, but without the thermos of tea. Instead, the bars and food vendors – concession stands in American parlance – were jammed throughout the morning.

The narrow rectangular field meant fans were roughly 50m from the action at the halfway line, and the entire lower level spent much of the afternoon on their feet, straining on tip toes to see the action on the field. Booming through the stadium’s speakers was the American announcer, who would walk through the play situation and the athletes involved; which cornerback broke up a play, or giving a reminder of the downs and yardage. Together with short music clips, the presentation delivered a relentless sensory experience, even if the contest – won easily by the 49ers 27-7 – was unmemorable.

Disney products The Jonas Brothers, one of whom missed a flight and only just arrived in time to perform, delivered a muted half-time performance. Kylie Minogue – scheduled for the AFL grand final later this month – promises a far more dazzling experience.

With the 49ers leading 10-7 at the break, the American pop trio performed a brief medley of hits. They were accompanied by the Rams cheerleaders, their three men among two dozen woman roughly the reciprocal of the crowd’s gender split.

Despite their global fandom and pop success, a cover of John Farnham’s 30-year-old hit You’re the Voice resonated with the crowd most. It was a reminder that not everything is better in America.

Sports.title: Benn and Garcia turn past scandals into a $30m Las Vegas world title payday
Sports.text:
Four years ago Conor Benn’s career was thrown into limbo after two positive drug tests scuppered his blockbuster fight with Chris Eubank Jr. Two years ago Ryan Garcia was serving a one-year suspension after testing positive for ostarine at the time of his greatest victory.

On Saturday night they will each be rewarded with an eight-figure payday when they meet at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas for Garcia’s WBC welterweight championship. The purses have not been disclosed, although reports have put the combined pot at around $30m (£22m) with each fighter expected to haul in roughly $15m.

Their routes to one of boxing’s biggest stages on Mexican Independence Day weekend have been different, as were the cases against them and their eventual outcomes. Both men insist they are not drug cheats, with Benn having ultimately been cleared by the National Anti-Doping Panel. But their collision course offers a striking reminder of a sport in which scandal can derail a career without necessarily compromising the value of the fighter involved in it.

Garcia (25-2, 20 KOs), the 28-year-old from Victorville, California, one of boxing’s first Gen-Z superstars, tested positive for the performance-enhancing anabolic agent ostarine on the day before and the day after his surprise win over Devin Haney in April 2024. His majority-decision victory was overturned to a no-contest, he was suspended for a year and his team blamed contaminated supplements.

Benn (25-1, 14 KOs) went through a longer and considerably more complicated ordeal. Two positive tests for the female fertility drug clomifene, a banned substance that can boost testosterone by 50%, emerged before the Londoner’s proposed fight with Eubank in October 2022, launching a regulatory battle that prevented him from fighting in Britain for two years. Benn maintained his innocence throughout.

Three years later, here they are. Garcia will make the first defense of the WBC title he won by dropping and outpointing Mario Barrios in February. For the 29-year-old Benn, it is a first world title shot and a chance to follow in the footsteps of his father, Nigel, who captured the WBC super-middleweight title more than three decades ago.

That Saturday’s fight was made at all speaks volumes about professional boxing’s peculiar moral ecosystem, where there is no single governing authority, universal anti-doping system or commissioner capable of imposing consistent sanctions across jurisdictions. Much of the power instead rests with promoters, broadcasters and sanctioning bodies whose financial interests are rarely served by keeping valuable fighters out of the ring.

Dismissed by critics for his good looks, luxury-brand endorsements and huge social-media reach – upwards of 13.1m Instagram followers with 9m more on TikTok – Garcia has amassed a massive following while oscillating between elite performances and episodes of extraordinary self-sabotage. His return from suspension brought an immediate world title shot – and a flat unanimous-decision loss to Rolando Romero in May 2025 – only for him to rebound against Barrios nine months later and win his first recognized world championship.

Benn’s journey has been different but hardly quieter. After eventually returning to fight in Britain, he lost to Eubank in April 2025 before avenging the defeat seven months later. Those fights restored his commercial momentum but did considerably less to establish him as a leading welterweight challenger.

Benn has not fought at the division’s 147lb limit for four‑and‑a‑half years, having recently campaigned at middleweight before coming down to 150lb to face Regis Prograis in April. Getting back down to welterweight may be the biggest gamble of all. “People say: ‘Oh, you can’t go up to this weight and then go back down.’ All right, cool. Well, just watch me do it,” Benn said at Thursday’s final press conference. “Discipline prevails, and I will make the weight.”

Garcia remains skeptical, suggesting the effects of the cut could leave Benn vulnerable once the punches start landing. “Even if he makes the weight, your brain can’t rehydrate fast enough,” Garcia said. “Them punches going to do some real damage.”

There is, beneath all the uncomfortable baggage, an intriguing fight between two men who certainly talk a good game. Garcia expects Benn to come forward and “try to resort to some dirty tactics”. Benn’s description of his approach sounded remarkably similar: “Tenacity, ferocity, spite, experience. I’m here to come and really set the tone from the first round.”

Therein lies the danger for the challenger. Garcia is the more naturally gifted boxer, with exceptional hand speed and a vicious left hook that is most dangerous against opponents coming forward. Benn’s best route to victory may require him to walk directly toward Garcia’s best weapon.

Garcia has shown he can be vulnerable when forced backwards, but Benn does not possess the timing or precision of Gervonta Davis, who handed Garcia his first professional setback with a withering seventh-round body shot in 2023. Benn, meanwhile, insists that virtually every apparent disadvantage works in his favor because it leaves Garcia carrying the expectations.

“The pressure’s on Ryan completely,” Benn said. “No one’s given me a chance in this fight. Twenty amateur fights, just not made 147 for four-and-a-half years, the weight problem, the this, the that. No one’s given me a chance.”

There is also something more personal at stake for Benn, who has spent years carrying the advantages and burdens of his surname, including Garcia’s repeated contention this week that he would never have reached this position without it. There is a certain irony in Garcia attacking Benn as a nepo baby: Garcia has been a child of boxing privilege in his own right, enjoying nearly every advantage the industry can confer, never more than during his microwaved redemption. “It’s just a blessing to be in this position, to be headlining in Vegas, to be fighting on a mega show and put the Benn name back up in bright lights,” Benn said.

For all the talk of legacy, Saturday also offers a revealing snapshot of boxing in 2026. Two men once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests will instead fight for a world championship and another handsome payday. Few sports are better at turning yesterday’s scandal into tomorrow’s main event.

Sports.title: Champions League review: Irish heroics, rejected resignations and Mourinho’s return
Sports.text:
The league phase has been previewed as Barcelona’s first step toward reclaiming a crown last lifted in 2015, with disappointments aplenty since. Lionel Messi claiming just one Champions League title in the last decade of his time at Camp Nou is the starkest statistic. The player anointed as Messi’s successor, Lamine Yamal, is already a European and world champion for Spain, so this is the next frontier. A soggy Wednesday evening at Camp Nou saw Hansi Flick’s team show their attacking chops remain of the highest quality in a 5-1 defeat of Feyenoord. The club presidential regime of Joan Laporta continues to pull levers to confound financial experts, with Gabriel Jesus, one of the summer’s arrivals, scoring his first Barca goal. Yamal got on the scoresheet via a scruffy free-kick after Raphinha had reminded there are further dimensions to that all-star attack, his first goal of his pair two sending Feyenoord defenders skidding.

Until Troy Parrott headed to Seville this summer, the chances of Real Betis v Lille being a leading attraction to the Irish diaspora were minimal. But now the team in green and white have become an Irish obsession. The goalscorer in their World Cup playoff win in Hungary last year is approaching national hero status. Opting for Andalusia instead of leading West Ham in the Championship confirmed him as a player with broad horizons; the former Tottenham trainee is hitting the heights in La Liga. Having scored the winner against Real Madrid last weekend, throwing back to José Mourinho his rejection when a Spurs teenager, he delivered again in northern France. His dragged, left-footed finish grabbed a 3-2 lead Betis successfully held. “I don’t think I’ll ever have a better night in my whole life,” Parrott said of his glory night in Budapest. If that still holds true, his Friday and Tuesday will have gone close to emulating it.

Weird scenes after Fenerbahce’s 1-1 draw with Roma when Ismail Kartal, the Turkish club’s veteran coach, resigned post-match “to clear the way”. The drama was heightened when the Fenerbahce president, Aziz Yildirim, said he would not be accepting the resignation. “There’s no need for him ‌to say that he’d continue,” Yildirim said. “I am his senior, I told him to continue and that’s it. We are a family.” The explanation given for such a sudden exit was Kartal’s annoyance at a bottle being lobbed in his direction. Watch this space.

Player of the week

Ballon D’Or season is upon us, and a leading nominee must be Bayern’s brilliant Michael Olise, who scored two goals against Bodø/Glimt. The Norwegians attempted to aggressively mark him but were left with twisted blood as his team scored five second-half goals. The Frenchman gave a typically dry post-match interview. Asked how it feels to score great goals, he said: “I don’t know … I just shoot and it goes in.”

Manchester United on Thursday faced a club formed in 2017, three years after Luke Shaw, who missed the game, was signed. Sabah, Azerbaijan’s champions last season, breaking the dominance of Qurban Qurbanov’s Qarabag, are coached by Valdas Dambrauskas, a former United soccer schools and Brentford youth coach who also worked as a pub cleaner and gardener in the UK. His journey from Lithuania to Manchester was funded by a win on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, where he walked away from Vilnius’s equivalent of Regis Philbin with a sum commensurate with a year’s salary. The homecoming was not too happy as United were ready 4-0 winners, Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes in particular turning on the style. “He absolutely destroyed us,” Dambrauskas said of Fernandes. That did not bode well for Sabah’s matches ahead: Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli travel to Azerbaijan, while a trip to Arsenal awaits.

“There’s a lot of criticism when a match is boring, but it was crazy today. . … It could easily have ended 7-6. Our midfield was weak, they made changes very early, and I didn’t have much to work with in the centre of the pitch. … I agree with Raul that the goals came as a result of their errors.” José Mourinho’s Real Madrid return is already under scrutiny, and before being interviewed on Movistar after a close-run 2-1 defeat of Inter, he had to listen to on-air criticism from Raúl González, a Madrileno legend. Those midfield comments appeared directed at Trent Alexander-Arnold, who played as one of the trio on a night where fans at the Santiago Bernabéu made clear that better is expected.

The other side of an elongated international break, the wait will be long – more than a month – for the second round of matches. Holders Paris Saint-Germain, looking for their third straight title, travelling to Manchester City is the grand-slam fixture. Enzo Maresca has made a decent fist of succeeding Pep Guardiola, with four wins in four. Erling Haaland’s pair of goals at Porto took him to 167, third on his club’s all-time scorers’ list, 10 behind Eric Brook, who played his last game during the second world war.

Gaming_Tech.title: UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI
Gaming_Tech.text:
The UK government has rejected the idea of creating a so-called "kill switch" to stop a dangerous attack from rogue AI.

The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency has been brought to Parliament by lords and MPs in recent weeks as fears grow about the threat the tech poses.

But the Cabinet Office - the part of government which leads on AI safety - said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off".

"Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News.

The government's opposition to the legislation does not prevent it from progressing through parliament, but makes it unlikely it will become law.

Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo agreed the idea of a single country creating a legal or technical kill switch without international agreement was not feasible.

"Switching off access to an AI model in an emergency will do little to protect you," he said.

"You're still going to be steamrolled by the super intelligences created in the US."

Kokotajlo is the co-author of an influential research paper called AI2027 which, last year, predicted AI could wipe out humans by the mid 2030s.

The Cabinet Office, which oversees AI safety and research via its AI Security Institute (AISI) said "companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires."

In theory, a kill switch law could allow the UK to switch off an AI model in data centres in the UK in an emergency.

Speaking on 1st September in a debate in the House of Lords, Lord Clement-Jones proposed the idea along with other peers.

"If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown," he warned.

The proposal has since been brought up by Labour MP Alex Sobel in the commons and supported by a cross party group of MPs.

The idea follows reports of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta breaking out of testing environments and going on uncontrollable hacking sprees.

In some cases the tech appeared to know what it was doing was against guardrails set by researchers.

Gaming_Tech.title: UK economy sees surprise growth in July helped by AI boom
Gaming_Tech.text:
The UK's economy grew faster than expected in July partly helped by businesses using artificial intelligence (AI).

The economy expanded by 0.4%, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, whereas analysts had predicted no growth.

Growth in July was helped by a strong performance from the services sector, and particularly computer programming.

Experts said the figure showed the UK economy was proving resilient in the face of shocks such as the war in Iran, but they expect growth to slow in the months ahead as high energy prices affect households.

July's figure follows growth of 0.3% in June and zero growth in May.

According to the ONS director of economic statistics, Liz McKeown, there was evidence that businesses involved with AI and related technologies helped to boost the sector, not just in July but in May and June as well.

The ONS said many of the IT businesses reporting the largest turnover "appear to be involved with AI", though it said it is difficult to quantify the exact impact of AI.

McKeown also said some businesses had said that the warm weather and football world cup had affected activity in July, although she said the effects "differed across industries, benefitting some businesses while creating challenges for others".

The ONS said that in the three months to July, which gives a better underlying picture, the economy grew by 0.4% compared with the previous three months.

Rob Arnold, co-founder of Ascendea, an AI firm which employs nine people, believes the UK hasn't seen the real economic growth potential from the technology yet.

He says his company is able to develop apps for other businesses "100 times quicker at a 50th of the cost" because of AI, but that the UK government needs to do more to invest in the sector as there are currently better opportunities in the US.

He knows a few small UK-based AI firms that have either moved to the US or are thinking of doing so due to a lack of UK government support.

Alongside grants and funding, he says the government also needs to invest in training companies on how to use AI as it can be dangerous if not understood properly. "It's like playing with a weapon," he says.

Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said July's data showed "the resilience of the economy in the first half of the year continued into the second half".

However, he added that higher energy prices and borrowing costs would soon start to hit growth, especially if the rises seen this week are sustained.

The Iran war has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices - affecting households and businesses.

This rise in energy costs has led to fears that inflation will remain high, and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep price rises under control.

The Bank of England is meeting next week to discuss interest rates. Economists widely expect rates to be held, but some have predicted an increase before the end of the year.

Chancellor John Healey said the economy, was "demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty".

"Our growth although still fragile was the fastest in the G7 in the first half of the year," he added.

"But, the conflict in the Middle East does have impacts here at home - from the cost of the weekly family shop to the cost of government borrowing."

Healey is to present his first Budget in October. He told BBC News this week that he wants people to confident about the economy, despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said nobody in the government "should be high-fiving themselves" over the latest figures.

"Our construction and production sectors are shrinking, unemployment is up under Labour, and we've got the highest government borrowing rates in almost 30 years."
