articles.title: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'
articles.text:
A top safety researcher at Anthropic has warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Evan Hubinger said in a post on X, external the risk from the models which currently exist was "low" but he was "worried" the technology might develop and improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.

He did not spell out how he thought AI systems could in future result in humans being wiped out.

But his comments are the latest in a series of increasingly stark warnings about AI, with the debate shifting from whether it truly poses a risk to how big that risk is.

Hubinger's intervention was in response to another post on X, external from Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who has just quit Anthropic and previously worked at OpenAI.

"Neither company is acting responsibly," he wrote.

"These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources."

OpenAI has been approached for comment.

Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who advises the UN on AI, told the BBC she was "shocked" by Hubinger and Coxon's social media posts.

She told the World at One on BBC Radio Four some of it could be "PR and marketing" however, as Anthropic and OpenAI raced towards highly anticipated stock market debuts.

But she added: "Why would someone want to say that? I would plead with investors not to invest in this company if that is their value system."

The resignation prompted Darren Jones, former chief secretary to the Treasury and chief secretary to Sir Keir Starmer, to write an open letter to Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling for a new multinational treaty for the safe development of AI.

He told the BBC governments had to come together to "collaborate" about what a treaty based on the development of superintelligence should look like.

"Unless governments take these warnings seriously enough and step up to it, the pace of development could mean that we end up with problems before we've started to look at whether it is an issue for us or not," he said.

Separately, the Financial Times reported, external Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI), one of the leading bodies in the world for assessing AI risk.

Anthropic has declined to comment on the posts by its employees or the situation with the AISI.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson did not comment on whether the latest model had been withheld from the AISI - instead saying it "continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, to make models safer".

In his post, which has been viewed more than 10 million times, Hubinger said "we really do earnestly believe" AI poses a species-ending risk to humans.

"I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to," he added.

Hubinger works in AI alignment, which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

Many leading researchers say those attempts appear to be failing, as demonstrated by a string of incidents this summer where AI agents - AI systems that are allowed to operate autonomously - carried out cyber-attacks.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all disclosed hacks carried out by their AI tools.

In Anthropic's safety report from August, external, it wrote there was a low risk of its models becoming misaligned with a hypothetical powerful organisation's desires, causing it to exploit or tamper with its systems.

It also said there was a similarly low risk of highly capable AI being able to "perform automated research and development" which could cause "catastrophic harm initiated by the AI". But it said it was "less confident in this assessment" than it was previously.

"We are seeing early signs of potential acceleration," it wrote.

Leading figures in the AI field have been raising the alarm about the safety threat the tech poses for years, with the heads of OpenAI, Google Deepmind and Anthropic saying as much in 2023.

But those warnings have become much more stark in recent weeks, as evidence emerges that firms may be struggling to control AI.

Earlier this month, OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called for "extreme caution" over AI's progress, warning more intervention may be needed to ensure "humans remain in control of the future".

Major figures in the space have been calling for AI development to be slowed in recent months, including Anthropic bosses Dario Amodei and Jared Kaplan.

In an open letter signed by 1,300 staff members of AI firms, external, they called for the US government to "support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development".

articles.title: White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern
articles.text:
The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use of the game's likeness.

The game, which saw players stack blocks to build a wall to "protect the border" is one of five arcade games which have appeared on the White House website.

On 4 September the official Tetris account on X posted, external the firm was "not involved in the creation" of the game and it took "copyright infringement very seriously".

The White House has not responded to requests for comment from the BBC or given an official reason for the takedown.

"At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and building people together, not dividing them," the firm said in its initial response to the game.

"To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community."

The Tetris Company has had previous success in suing firms for infringing on its copyright - settling for an undisclosed fee with the makers of the iPhone game Mino in 2012, which it claimed stole the look and feel of the block-builder.

Four other arcade games still remain on the mini-game section of the White House website.

"Flappy Bill", a clone of the 2013 viral hit Flappy Bird sees players fly a bald eagle and dodging monuments from the National Mall.

Meanwhile in Rio Run, players must "patrol the line along the river", with gameplay reminiscent of the classic phone game Snake.

articles.title: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India: report
articles.text:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse

Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found.

The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India.

Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP), external says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year.

When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement."

The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings.

About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials.

After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter.

The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children.

When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations.

The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children.

But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough.

Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material

"Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu.

The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC.

According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act.

TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad.

According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year.

In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website, external about how it fights child exploitation on its apps.

"Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said.

TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live.

For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards."

For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad.

When the BBC reached out to Meta for a comment, they said, "we've built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something: that's why many of the ads flagged to us had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under $5,000".

TTP said that when it reached out to Meta for a response, all the ads they reported were removed.

This was similar to what happened during the BBC's investigation. When the BBC used Meta's reporting system to report one of the ads featuring child sexual abuse to Instagram, the platform did not take it down.

Later, when the BBC asked Meta for comment, it said it had already disabled several adverts and suspended the accounts posting them. The company said it had removed additional ads, disabled more accounts and blocked URLs for other content that violated its policies in response to the BBC's findings.

TTP said that the vast majority of the 332 ads they found directed users to AI image or video generation apps, mostly from Chinese developers.

The report alleged that by advertising these apps using images of child sexual abuse, the implication is that they can be used for creating or viewing CSAM.

Meta has said it prohibits, external promotion of nudify apps, which use AI to create fake non-consensual nude or sexually explicit images.

One of India's top cyber police officers, Shikha Goel, who is director of the Cyber Security Bureau in the Indian state of Telangana, told the BBC that one of the biggest challenges with CSAM is "the ease with which users can move from one platform to another, making it harder to nab them".

"We are hopeful that the government will be addressing this in its latest interactions with social media intermediaries and direct them accordingly," she added.

The ads that BBC had found in its investigation also directed users to another app - the messaging app Telegram - where they could buy the material for as little as 99 rupees [$1.05; £0.80].

Telegram told the BBC at the time that the company uses both automated and human moderation to tackle CSAM, and that it has "virtually eliminated the public spread of CSAM" on its platform.

Ads on Meta's platforms are only published after first being approved by its moderation technology. Its review system relies primarily on automation and is designed to check images, video, text and audio, as well as who the ad is targeting and where links send them to.

After the BBC's investigation, Meta had said that "no system is perfect" and that "determined criminals continue to try to exploit our platform, including through our advertising systems".

But TTP found that several of the ads featuring child sexual abuse were placed by Meta's own ad agency partners in China.

These partners, known as "resellers", channel billions of dollars' worth of Chinese advertising onto Facebook and Instagram. The partners did not respond to TTP's questions.

TTP said that new ads have continued to appear even after they made Meta aware of their report's findings. They shared details of 17 ads including 11 that ran in India on 1-2 September.

articles.title: Should promotion depend on how workers use AI?
articles.text:
It's in Duncan Trevithick's interest to be good at using AI at work - if he can use it to get more tasks done, faster, he'll qualify for a bonus at the end of the year.

On the surface, it's a great incentive. But he's questioning what's really in it for him.

"The uncomfortable interpretation is that employees are being assessed on how effectively they can participate in their own redundancy," says Spain-based Trevithick, 34, who works in marketing for an AI training data company.

But if he uses AI to take care of two days worth of work each week, he says the financial rewards don't add up.

"I do not receive two days off or a 40% pay rise. The higher output simply becomes the new baseline. In the short term, that may help me get promoted. In the longer term, I have helped prove how much of my job no longer requires me," he says.

"I'm just trying to view myself as a manager, and I'm managing some people, and I'm also managing AI agents, or AI loops, or whatever you want to call it."

Using employees' AI abilities as a measure of whether they should get a bonus, promoted - or even sacked - is fast becoming more common.

Accenture CEO Julie Sweet told the Rapid Response podcast in March: "Today, AI at Accenture is how we do work. So if you want to get promoted, you've got to do the things that we do in order to operate at Accenture."

And big names like Disney, Meta, JP Morgan and KPMG have introduced "AI leaderboards" to track and rank employees' usage of the array of LLMs and platforms at their disposal, according to media reports, external. Crypto trading platform Coinbase has already fired engineers who didn't complete AI training, as requested by the chief executive, Brian Armstrong, external.

It demonstrates how eager business leaders are to see a return from their AI investments, especially when 94% of companies have yet to see significant value from AI, according to a report, external by consultants McKinsey.

Employees feel they have to get on board, thanks to the current state of the jobs market - in the UK, vacancies have hit a five-year low.

Meanwhile, 75% of the 1,881 UK jobseekers polled in July by recruiter Gi Group say they would not be put off applying to an organisation that had introduced AI proficiency into individual performance reviews. Around 22% said it would be off-putting.

"It's like being in the sea and you see a giant wave coming. You can get out a surfboard and try and ride it as long as possible, or you can just let it take you under. But you can't stop the wave," says Trevithick.

But what's going on at the large consultancy Pamela (her name has been changed to protect her identity) works for isn't sitting right with her.

She's a US-based senior executive who has observed that, while there isn't a formal mandate for employees to use AI, it's obviously determining who is rewarded, and who is left behind.

"The ground is shifting under us. You've got to demonstrate [AI] fluency and fluidity as one of your key achievements. It's kind of quiet where nobody's saying, 'learn AI or else'. But let me tell you, in performance reviews, they reward who uses it well," says Pamela.

That shift, she adds, means that AI capabilities are now counting for more than actual experience, which is creating a "two tier workforce".

"You've got the same job title, same tenure, but different value based on whether someone treats AI as a threat or a tool - that gap widens really quickly once leadership notices it," says Pamela.

"AI fluency beats credentials every day. Somebody that has 15, 20 years of experience and no AI fluency will be passed over for those that have, say, three years, but are fast with the tools."

She adds: "If you're not visibly using AI, you see slower promotion timelines. It's harder to be seen, and it's harder to fight being on that shortlist."

But is it legal for companies to shift the goal posts like this?

Legally, bosses are in the clear, confirms Tina Chander, partner and employment lawyer at Weightmans. But she says it does open up questions about pay and fairness.

"The question then becomes whether the employer increases expectations on the basis that the employee can now produce more work. Is that fair?" questions Chander.

"And if an employee is effectively doing more because AI has made them more efficient, should they be rewarded differently? Or are they effectively making themselves redundant, thus acting as a disincentive to be productive?"

Chander advises businesses to have clear policies, training and boundaries in place, otherwise they risk employees opening up disputes about fairness, performance expectations and job security.

Indeed, from January 2027, UK employees will have six months to submit unfair dismissal claims compared with the current three months, and will be able to do so after just six months service, rather than the current two years.

Yet HR consultant Tina Rahman says employers aren't currently being transparent enough in telling employees why they want AI to be part of people's jobs, and what the end purpose of that is - which she agrees is to save costs and time, but also to cut down on outsourcing.

"Because they misunderstand it, this is not being reflected to employees," says Rahman, who runs a London-based consultancy, HR Habitat.

A lack of clarity around AI usage is certainly causing discontent at Pamela's company.

"Leadership is being inconsistent and vague on purpose. Firms want productivity gains without owning the disruption narrative," she says.

"If something goes wrong, they're going to say, 'I didn't tell you to do that. Where'd you get that from?' Then if you did something with AI, and it works, great."

Mandating AI use at work can become purely performative, rather than having any real positive impact, warns Kamila Miller, applied AI researcher and lecturer at Henley Business School.

"Make AI usage a KPI [key performance indicator], and people will log their interactions to hit the metric, route work through a chatbot that did not need it, and generate AI-flavoured outputs that look productive on a dashboard. You will measure adoption. You will not measure judgement, learning, or better decisions," states Miller, who is based in Reading.

"You have not made people more skilled - you have made them more obedient."

Some firms have acknowledged those arguments.

In April, Luis von Ahn, the CEO of Duolingo, told the podcast Silicon Valley Girl, external that his language learning firm is no longer using AI use as part of performance reviews.

"We found that people... were asking: 'Do you want us to use AI for AI's sake?'

"In the end we backtracked and we said: 'Look, the most important thing for your performance is that you are doing, whatever your job is, as well as possible. A lot of times AI can help you with that. But if it can't, I'm not going to force you to do that.'"

Meanwhile, in May, the Financial Times reported, external that Amazon had shut down an internal leaderboard which tracked employee's use of AI. The report said employees had been attempting to climb the rankings by setting AI needless tasks.

Despite those high-profile moves, some staff still they need to show AI proficiency - Pamela is one of those.

In her mid 50s, she plans to retire within 10 years, and wants to keep her job so she doesn't risk losing any pension and health benefits. She's visibly stepping up how AI is helping her bring in new clients, and making sure she's being credited for it.

As for Duncan Trevithick, he's doing his best to future proof himself with a number of side projects.

"If AI can do a job better than you can, it makes sense for the business to replace you. That's how the capitalist model works. So it's about, how can you move into a position where you own assets where you can leverage AI, and then you benefit," says Trevithick.

articles.title: OpenAI says it cracked 90-year-old maths problem in 88 hours
articles.text:
OpenAI says it has found a solution to a decades-old advanced maths problem in a matter of hours using a new artificial intelligence (AI) model and thousands of AI bots.

The ChatGPT-maker said on Tuesday, external that by focusing a group of roughly 10,000 AI agents, or AI bots that undertake tasks somewhat autonomously, it solved a notoriously difficult maths problem in just 88 hours.

The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, external, which concern how fluids move. For 90 years important aspects of the problems have lacked a proof, the argument underlying a correct math equation.

OpenAI called the solution which it found a "milestone" and evidence that AI tools are improving quickly.

OpenAI's solution has yet to be verified independently or publicly accepted by The Clay Mathematics Institute, a maths organisation based in the US which runs the Millennium Prize that offers big money to the first to solve certain mathematical conundrums.

But the company's claim has already sparked a backlash.

Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematics professor at New York University, said on Tuesday, external that he and Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working for OpenAI rival Anthropic, had also been working on solving the problem.

The duo had been using OpenAI's tool Codex in their work. But Buckmaster said that on 3 September, he found out that "information about our progress had been passed to OpenAI".

Buckmaster's statement came the same day, but hours before, OpenAI published its Navier–Stokes work. He claimed that OpenAI did not begin working on the Navier–Stokes equations until "after information about our work had reached OpenAI". He included text from emails exchanged with OpenAI over the work and his questions of the company's timing and methods.

Buckmaster added that he had not yet read OpenAI's full proof, but felt compelled to go public with "what I was told, when, and what was proposed to me...because the alternative is to let a sequence of announcements say something I know to be false".

OpenAI on Tuesday congratulated the "concurrent work" of Buckmaster and Alpöge, calling it "remarkable".

The company said it had not seen "any of their work through any means until they released it publicly" and that no user data was accessed in its work on the Navier–Stokes problem.

"While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models⁠", the company added. "However, our proofs differ significantly and even the precise results proved are different."

OpenAI said that, at the end of August, it started to train a new model that quickly showed that it was adept at maths. AI models are computer programs trained on huge amounts of data to recognise and predict patterns in information.

While the new OpenAI model remains a tool only used within the company, as it is "significantly more capable" than the company's most recent AI model release, its researchers decided to use it on certain notable advanced maths problems.

OpenAI admitted that last week on 1 September, it had "heard rumours that two Millennium Prize problems had been resolved" and so decided to put thousands of AI bots trained on the new internal model to work attempting to solve some of the remaining problems.

By Sept 5, or roughly 88 hours after it had set 10,000 AI bots to the task, OpenAI had found a solution to what's referred to as the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem.

The problem is at the heart of turbulence, which is a phenomenon that is still not well understood.

Although it took the AI bots seemingly little time to reach a solution, OpenAI said the bots exchanged nearly 3 million messages and used up 130 billion output tokens, or the individual lines of text and code an AI model produces in answers, on Navier–Stokes alone.

Such an effort would have cost roughly $10m (£7.3m), based on OpenAI's own pricing, external for output from its most advanced models.

The solution that OpenAI says it has now reached for the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem resolved two out of the four statements in the proof that the Millennium Prize had demanded. The prize is worth $1m to a winner.

"Our goal in releasing this result is to report on the substantial progress of our AI models," OpenAI said on Tuesday. "We do not intend to claim the Millennium Prize for this result."

articles.title: The Voice UK: Alesha Dixon and Stacey Solomon joing show as ITV confirms revamp
articles.text:
Alesha Dixon and Stacey Solomon are to host The Voice UK as part of a revamp of the show announced by ITV.

The pair replace Emma Willis, who has presented the singing contest since 2014 but recently left to front the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.

ITV also confirmed earlier reports that singer Cheryl and rapper Aitch will join the The Voice as coaches, sitting in the show's famous giant red chairs.

It comes after Sir Tom Jones said earlier this week that he had been removed from the series despite wanting to stay, over an insurance issue.

On Friday, the network said: "ITV would like to thank the irreplaceable Sir Tom Jones for all his years on The Voice UK, and the countless incredible and unforgettable moments he gave the show.

"He has brought joy to audiences, and to every singer who performed for him and with him."

The changes will take effect from the next series, which began filming on Friday. The series currently airing on ITV was filmed in 2025.

Destiny's Child singer Kelly Rowland will remain on The Voice coaching panel, alongside Black Eyed Peas frontman Will.I.Am, who has been on the show since its first series.

On Wednesday, Sir Tom, 86, said in a statement he had been offered a "much-reduced role" on the series, which he was "not thrilled about".

"The reason given is because of a financial difficulty with insurance," he added. "They now say in the press they wanted to 'refresh' the show, and with a new coaching line-up there wouldn't be a chair for me."

He concluded: "The only thing I know right now is that there's never a good time to fire an 86-year-old who's still pretty good at his job."

Cheryl launched her career with pop group Girls Aloud and later had several chart hits as a solo artist. She has recorded several songs with Will.I.Am.

She also served as a judge on ITV's The X Factor when the singing competition was at the peak of its popularity in the late 2000s.

Aitch is a Manchester-born rapper whose hits include Rain, Baby, War and Taste (Make It Shake).

"Fusing legendary industry experience with a vibrant competitive spirit, our latest panel of icons is ready to discover and celebrate the most remarkable and exciting vocal talent emerging from every corner of the country," ITV said.

Dixon shot to fame as a member of girl group Mis-Teeq and has served as judge on Strictly Come Dancing and Britain's Got Talent.

She has previously hosted The Greatest Dancer and the Eurovision Song Contest when it was hosted by the UK in Liverpool in 2023.

Solomon came second on The X Factor in 2009, and is now known for hosting Sort Your Life Out and appearing on reality show Stacey & Joe with her husband Joe Swash.

The Voice launched its UK version in 2012, hosted by Holly Willoughby and Reggie Yates, after the format was successful in the US.

Willis took over presenting duties in 2014, joined for several series by Marvin Humes of boyband JLS. The show jumped from the BBC to ITV in 2017.

The show differs from other singing competitions in that the coaches have their backs turned to contestants as they audition.

If the coaches like a contestant's voice, they can spin around in their chairs to see their identity and offer to mentor them during the series.

Other previous coaches on the UK series include Olly Murs, Jennifer Hudson, Kylie Minogue, Rita Ora, Anne Marie and LeAnn Rimes.

articles.title: Esther Rantzen says she is too fragile to travel to Switzerland to end life
articles.text:
Dame Esther Rantzen has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.

The veteran broadcaster, 86, said she would have to fly to the country, where the practice is legal, alone, which she could only have done before her life became "unbearable" and before she was ready to end her life.

The Childline founder, who is terminally ill with cancer, first revealed in December 2023 that she had joined the Dignitas clinic.

Dame Esther used her statement on Thursday to reiterate a plea for MPs to vote in favour of legalising assisted dying in England and Wales when proposed legislation is revisited by Parliament on Friday.

She announced she had joined Dignitas about a year after being diagnosed with stage four lung cancer.

"Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest," she said.

"And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.

"So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance."

Dame Esther added that "everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now", with loved ones either unable to visit her or "see me suffering pain or indignity" when they do.

The prominent assisted dying campaigner said the law - which she described as "messy and cruel" - must "change and change quickly".

Helping someone end their life is currently considered a criminal offence across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Jersey legalised assisted dying for terminally ill adults earlier this year.

MPs are considering a draft law that, if passed, would make it legal in England and Wales under specific circumstances for people who are terminally ill with less than six months to live.

While Dame Esther, who is best known for presenting the BBC programme That's Life! for 21 years, is among several leading figures in favour of the bill, there are also campaigners against it, including Paralympian Baroness Grey-Thompson

They fear that a change in the law could mean that disabled and other vulnerable people could be pressured to end their lives, while also criticising the wording of the proposed legislation as not providing strong enough safeguards.

The bill has been through several drafts and has been scrutinised by several Parliamentary committees and the House of Lords, which submitted 1,200 amendments.

The bill was previously introduced in 2024, but the last session of Parliament ran out of time before it was passed.

It was reintroduced in this Parliament and a second vote will be held on Friday afternoon. If it passes the House of Commons, rarely invoked powers could be used, meaning it would not need the assent of the Lords to become law this time.

Proponents of the bill have indicated they would try to bring legislation again as soon as possible were it to be voted down on Friday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would not be voting on the issue and has suggested that palliative and social care should be better funded before legalising assisted suicide is considered.

Assisted dying is legal in a number of countries - including Canada, Australia and Belgium - as well as in Switzerland, though the circumstances under which it is legal differ between those nations.

articles.title: Oxford museum agrees to return remains to Naga ancestral homeland
articles.text:
More than three dozen sets of human remains taken during the British colonial rule of India and Myanmar are set to be returned to their ancestral home by a museum.

Skulls and bones belonging to the Naga people of northeastern India and Myanmar - formerly known as Burma - have been displayed at the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford for more than a century.

In 2020, the museum removed all human remains from public display as part of what the it called a "decolonisation process" - including the ancestral Naga remains.

The museum has now announced that a formal decision has been made by the University of Oxford Council to return the 39 ancestral human remains to their homeland.

"They've been here in a foreign land for more than a century," Dr Vihuto Asumi, President of the Sumî Hoho Naga tribe, said of the remains.

"We believe that their spirits are still not at rest - so by doing this, we believe it will bring spiritual healing, not only to the ancestral remains here but to everyone who died during the head-hunting days."

articles.title: Practical Magic 2's Maisie Williams: People long for simpler times
articles.text:
Mix together a beloved film simmering for decades, a sprinkling of social media hype and a generous glug of star power and you just might conjure up the long-awaited sequel to Practical Magic.

The 1998 fantasy romcom, starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as witchy sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, received mixed reviews from critics when it was first released.

But it's put a spell on a new generation discovering it online, with some now regarding the film as a cult classic and autumn staple.

The demand for a follow-up by this new wave of fans helped convince Bullock and Kidman to reprise their roles nearly 30 years on, they say.

"You never get the opportunity to do something where people really are asking you, 'please do it'," says Bullock. "It's usually us going to them."

Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast this time round to play Sally's daughters, Kylie and Antonia.

Kissing Booth star King tells BBC Newsbeat she feels this desire for nostalgic content, which has become one of the defining forces within entertainment in recent years, has been influenced by "the world moving so fast".

"I think with technology moving at the speed that it is, we're really missing the times when we were less reachable," she says.

"If we couldn't figure out something, we'd stare out the window until it came to us, and I think we're nostalgic for a time like that."

She feels this can also be a strength of cinema as it can help "make memories" and "feelings" for people that they can revisit by rewatching.

The upcoming release comes at a time when reboots, reunions and remakes are dominating film and TV lists.

Game of Thrones star Williams agrees the drive for nostalgic content feels like a "symptom of people longing for simpler times", but says she is "very grateful" that they have made a sequel and not a remake.

"I do believe in pushing the story forwards and I do believe in telling new stories," she says.

"And I do believe stories can come back around and they can still be meaningful.

"But I am not the biggest fan of the remake because I think it's a shame to withhold ourselves from telling a new story."

Practical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic with the characters once again confronting a family curse which condemns anyone who loves and is loved by an Owens woman to death.

There are also nods to the original throughout, with bubbling family tension, dark romantic "witchcore" fashion and the iconic midnight margaritas.

US acting stalwarts Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing return to their roles for the follow-up, while Guardians of the Galaxy actor Lee Pace, Cobra Kai's Xolo Maridueña and House of the Dragon's Solly McLeod are new additions.

Reviews so far have been mixed, with the Guardian describing it as a "nostalgia-bait return", external which is as "strange and messy as the first" but with "warm seasonal pleasures to be had".

Meanwhile The Hollywood Reporter, external says the "slapdash" sequel "works better the less you look for any sense of logic, and the more you just lean into the transient joys of watching these actresses bounce off each other".

articles.title: Bayeux Tapestry unveiled to UK public for first time at British Museum
articles.text:
The Bayeux Tapestry has gone on public display in the UK for the first time since it was created nearly 1,000 years ago.

It was originally embroidered in England but kept for centuries in France, and tells the story of the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

The 70m (230ft)-long 11th Century tapestry is being loaned to the British Museum while its usual home in Normandy, France undergoes renovation.

Doors at the museum opened at 10:00 BST, with shield-wielding re-enactors in costumes from the era waiting outside.

It's a loan almost 100 years in the making, but despite some opposition in France to it being moved, the French Culture minister recently said it arrived in a "wonderful state".

History buffs arrived early en masse to catch a glimpse of the opening.

Adrian Harris told BBC News that it was a "real privilege" to be one of the first members of the public to see the tapestry in England.

"I'm not a very emotive or expressive person but I was absolutely blown away by it," he said, moments after seeing the tapestry.

He described how he was taken aback when he had an uninterrupted view of it at the top of stairs at the start of the exhibition.

Serena Smith took a tour inside the museum before her slot at 11:30 BST.

When she bought her ticket, she was 4,000th in the queue, despite clicking on a link moments after receiving an email from the British Museum.

"I want you to write that I was first in the queue [today]," she stressed.

Armed with 24 pages of annotated notes, she said she was looking forward to trying to recognise the Normans from their round haircuts, and seeing their boats on board the ships they use to reach the English shores.

Cecilia and Fabio Zanini were completely wowed by the scale of the Bayeux Tapestry.

"I was amazed by the vibrancy of the colours. The detail of the characters," Cecilia said. "It gave both of us goosebumps."

Fabio said he was constantly looking left and right to see all the action and he was surprised by the scale of the tapestry, particularly the number of Norman boats and cavalry.

"It feels like you're in the battlefield," he added, praising the "real sense of movement" in the embroidery.

"It really allowed you to go back to 1066."

But others told the BBC the event was "out of reach" because of its cost and London location.

Angie in Leeds said the "historic event" was "out of reach for many, many families in the north" when you factor in the cost of train tickets and food costs on top of the museum tickets themselves.

"London-only cultural events alienate many families north of Watford," she added.

Another man spoke of the "extreme queuing" required to view the exhibit. Hadyn Blakeston said he felt like he was on a "conveyor belt" while moving along the tapestry.

"It's one long queue," he said. "I know we're supposed to love queuing, but it was extreme queuing."

Michael Lewis, one of the four curators for the exhibition, told the Press Association: "1066 is, of course, one of the most important events in English history, and the tapestry is the ultimate reflection of that in terms of a visual narrative.

"Some people see it as akin to a graphic novel or a cartoon or something like that, it's immediately recognisable."

He described France allowing it to come to the UK and be displayed at the British Museum as "an enormous act of diplomacy".

Tickets to the exhibition are sold out until the next release on 21 October.

The Bayeux Tapestry is at the British Museum until 11 July 2027.

articles.title: Female DJs call out intimidation and sexual harassment
articles.text:
Female DJs have described experiencing "blatant misogyny", harassment and intimidation while performing and said women are often treated as "guests" rather than professionals behind the decks.

Anna McAteer, Andrea Shearer and Julie Dunne have all spoken about experiences ranging from unwanted interference with equipment and inappropriate comments to physical intimidation.

They said the problem reflects wider attitudes towards women working in nightlife, rather than being the fault of the venues and promoters themselves.

Shearer said she had "never really seen it happen to a male colleague".

"I just still think that there's a bit of an attitude that women are somehow guests in the space rather than DJs that have earned their place there," she said.

"Whereas whenever it comes to a man in the booth, it's just not even a question."

She said women face a different level of scrutiny and unwanted attention simply because they were performing.

Shearer said she was subjected to online abuse earlier this year when a man from Belfast posted about her on Facebook, calling her a poor DJ and claiming that she only received gigs because she was a woman.

She said he also falsely claimed she performed sexual favours to obtain bookings.

"It's just insane to have someone kind of boil all of my hard work that I've done towards this down to who I've slept with," she said.

"And it's just blatant misogyny."

She also pointed to comments aimed at female DJs on social media, where discussions about their music can be overshadowed by comments about their appearance.

"It's 2026, grow up. She's doing her job."

McAteer, an up-and-coming Belfast DJ who has played at venues across Northern Ireland, including AVA Festival, said she had repeatedly experienced people entering the DJ booth or interfering with her set.

She said during one recent performance a man came up behind her and started rewinding one of the decks.

She described it as the fourth incident of its kind in about a year.

On another occasion she said a man had to be removed from the booth three times before returning and scrolling through the USB containing her music.

"He was just insisting that he's a DJ as well," she said.

McAteer said the behaviour also creates a safety issue.

"I've been quite lucky not to have too many physical encounters whenever I've been playing, but one did stand out to me."

She recalled an incident involving an older man who approached her while she was DJing and began asking explicit questions before touching her equipment.

McAteer said it is "very uncomfortable and it's just, in my opinion, not on".

For Julie Dunne, the experience of being intimidated while performing eventually led her to stop DJing in bars.

She said an incident during a Christmas gig began when a man approached her to request a song she did not have.

"I was really polite to him and said, 'Look, I apologise, I don't have it on me'," she said.

The man became aggressive and kept demanding her to play the song. When she apologised again he began screaming and swearing at her, calling her "pathetic" and terrible at her job.

"It got quite physical, he was up in my face and I was in tears."

Dunne said the experience made her question whether she should continue to take bookings.

She believes the issue extends beyond DJs, with female photographers, lighting technicians, bar workers and other women working in nightlife also experiencing inappropriate behaviour.

Dunne said while both men and women can face disruption while working, the nature of the incidents women experience can be different.

"When it's actual physical intimidation or sexual harassment, it's not the same at all."

Despite their experiences, the DJs were keen to stress that they did not blame the venues or promoters involved.

McAteer said venues and staff had "always went above and beyond" when they became aware of an incident and continued to check on her whenever she returned to venues, even as a customer.

However, she believes "the real issue is the societal attitude towards DJing, towards female DJs".

She said people should understand that DJs are working and that entering a booth without permission can be intimidating and potentially dangerous.

"That man that invaded my stage should never have been there three or four more times," she said.

Colin Neill, Chief Executive of Hospitality Ulster, said the industry takes a "zero-tolerance approach" to misogynistic, intimidating, threatening or inappropriate behaviour.

"Everyone has the right to enjoy a night out and to work in our sector without feeling unsafe, intimidated, or harassed."

Neill said hospitality businesses had an important role in creating safe environments and that Hospitality Ulster works with the Ending Violence Against Women and Girls team at Stormont.

He also highlighted the Ask for Angela initiative, which provides a discreet way for anyone who feels unsafe or uncomfortable in a venue to seek assistance from trained staff.

articles.title: Strictly: New hosts explain their roles as they reject 'roving presenter' reports
articles.text:
Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe have said they will not have "fixed roles" on Strictly Come Dancing, as they prepare to replace Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman later this month.

Daly and Winkleman left the programme together at the end of the 2025 series.

Daly was the host on the dancefloor, introducing the dancers and judges, while Winkleman did the post-dance debrief upstairs in the "Clauditorium".

"No one's replacing anybody - at the minute it's all very kind of open," Willis told Richard Osman on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.

They also scotched reports of Radebe having a "roving reporter" role , externalon the show, with Willis saying: "There's definitely no backstage roving reporter, which is what has been reported quite a bit."

Widdicombe added that they would "be like Total Football" [where players can take the role of anyone on the team], adding: "We're going to be moving everywhere".

Radebe added he will definitely be doing "a little bit of prying and finding out the truth", having been a professional dancer on the show, with the advantage of knowing everyone on it really well already.

He called his new role "very, very exciting," although he admitted he felt a "little bit of a tinge" of FOMO [fear of missing out] at seeing the pros in rehearsals.

They also added that the plan to put the three of them together was a "wild card decision" by producers, which took them all by surprise.

Willis explained the audition process, saying they had to do a "chemistry test" to see how they interacted as a group.

She said they were told: "This is the last one and this is a wild card. We're just like, 'What happens if we do three?'

"And they said, 'It's so much of a wild card, we don't really have a script for you either.

"'So we're going to sit down, get it up on the screen and we'll have a little tinker all together'."

articles.title: Harry Styles extends tour, with Kylie as a support act
articles.text:
Harry Styles is extending his record-breaking Together, Together tour in 2027, with 25 more shows, including a return to Wembley Stadium next August.

The singer, who is currently in the middle of a 30-show residency at New York's Madison Square Garden, is adding dates in Ireland, Spain, Italy, Germany and France - who all missed out on the tour's first leg this summer.

Every city will see a different support act, with 80s pop icons Tears For Fears playing at Wembley, and pop legend Kylie Minogue on the bill in Los Angeles.

Although Minogue is a festival headliner in Europe, these shows will represent her first ever stadium concerts in the US.

She celebrated the announcement on her Instagram stories, writing: "Together, together. Harry. Me. Can't wait to see you in April, LA."

Unlike the first half of the tour, which concentrated on long residencies in cities like London and New York, the 2027 dates represent a more traditional rolling stage show.

Styles will also play US stadiums for the first time as a solo artist - with dates booked in Phoenix, Dallas, Atlanta and Chicago.

After confusion and outcry over ticket prices for the 2026 shows, the singer's team have made the pricing structure clear for his upcoming dates, specifying that prices will range from $60 to $300 (£44 to £221).

The 2027 dates will also introduce "Unpredictable Fun Tickets," an initiative to make concerts more accessible to people on a limited income.

The programme will make a limited number of tickets available for £20 in the UK, $20 in the US and €20 in Europe. Details on availability and how to apply will be announced soon.

The cost of regular tickets will vary by city. Details, including on-sale dates, are available on the star's website., external

Fans were already aware that a second leg of Styles' tour was on the way, after the 32-year-old posted a note on Wednesday teasing what he called the "final" shows of the hugely-successful run.

"When we decided to do the 2026 tour I knew it would be special but what you turned it into was far beyond what I could have imagined," he wrote.

"I love playing music, I love being with all of you and being a part of the love and joy you all create together every night. That's why I wanted you to be the first to know we will be adding 2027 dates, which honestly, at first I found daunting.

"Being an artist is the only life I've ever known really, I have been doing this since I was 16 years old, and I feel like the luckiest person in the world to still be sharing these moments with you.

"Tomorrow's announcement will be the final cities of Together, Together," he continued.

"After that, I don't know what comes next for me, but I know that I'm excited to find out."

articles.title: Drag Race UK: BBC drops Ru Paul show after eight series
articles.text:
RuPaul's Drag Race UK is leaving the BBC after eight series, the broadcaster has confirmed.

A spokesperson for the broadcaster said it was facing "very difficult choices" in the face of "significant financial pressures".

The show is currently broadcast on BBC Three and iPlayer. Future series - as well as its spin-off vs The World - will be broadcast on Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.

At its peak, the UK version of the international drag competition averaged at around 1.5 million viewers per episode.

A spokesperson for the BBC said it was "proud [...] of this groundbreaking show" and thanked "RuPaul, World of Wonder and everyone involved, both on and off screen".

Started in 2019, Drag Race UK brought British drag into mainstream entertainment in the UK, and has made household names of drag performers such as La Voix, Danny Beard, and Tia Kofi.

The show sees drag queens compete in a series of challenges to impress judges RuPaul, Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Alan Carr, and often features big name celebrity guest judges.

It has become a staple of LGBTQ+ culture and has been praised for its portrayal of the distinct style of British drag.

The corporation is currently rolling out plans to make £500m of savings, with director-general Matt Brittin previously telling staff "the scale of savings requires tough choices".

A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly."

Announcing the news on Instagram, Wow Presents Plus said a "new era" of Drag Race UK was on the way.

A new series, Drag Race UK All Stars, which sees previous fan favourites return to compete again, will premiere in Autumn 2027 exclusively on Wow Presents Plus.

BBC News understands the current series of Drag Race UK, which launched in September 2026, will continue to air as normal on BBC Three and appear on iPlayer, and all existing series will continue to be available once the move is complete.

Tia Kofi, the winner of RuPaul's Drag Race UK vs The World series 2 in 2024, stated that the programme has, until now, provided a platform for performers who otherwise lack mainstream representation.

The performer told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday that cutting the show also means a "marginalised" audience now has nowhere to go.

"I think the mistake is that they seem to be dropping programmes that they consider to be for more niche audiences, which I just don't think makes a lot of logical sense because the niche audiences are the ones who are very much staying on and watching these things," the Drag Queen and singer said.

"But particularly when it comes to programs like Drag Race UK or the cancellation of I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl, or the Rap Game UK on the BBC as well, the more marginalised audiences have limited representation in mainstream media.

"[They] offer people a platform when they wouldn't have that. There aren't really those alternatives for drag performers in the UK."

Last year's runner-up Elle Vosque told BBC Newsbeat that taking the show off the BBC where it's "accessible to everyone" would make it more challenging for people to discover drag.

"You could be flicking through the BBC and fall upon the show and end up loving it and it could be totally not something that you've been exposed to before – so I think that is the biggest downside," she said.

Fan Alex Re agrees, saying: "For that young queer kid sat at home wanting a community, wanting something to relate to, that's now behind something they have to pay for.

"It feels like we're losing that kind of access, it's a worry that kids aren't going to have that."

The BBC does represent the LGBQT+ community through storylines in shows including Mr Loverman, Rob & Rylan's Grand Tour, Amandaland, EastEnders, What It Feels Like For a Girl, The Dickie Show, Vigil, Smoggie Queens, Such Brave Girls and Juice.

The corporation declined to comment on whether future series of other international versions of the show, including Drag Race Canada and Drag Race Down Under, would continue to air.

Earlier this year, the BBC announced it was dropping LGBTQ+ dating show I Kissed a Boy - which made history as the UK's first gay dating show - and I Kissed a Girl.

Jordan Burrow, a contestant on series two of I Kissed a Boy, said the decision was an example of "where we're at within the queer community".

The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges".

articles.title: The Odyssey and Spider-Man propel record-breaking summer box office worldwide
articles.text:
As well as celebrating their wedding, the actors Tom Holland and Zendaya have something else to toast: their two summer blockbusters – The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day – have officially made box office history.

The films were credited as the driving force behind the US’s biggest summer season of all time, taking $4.761bn (£3.51bn) from 1 May-7 September, beating 2013’s $4.756bn.

Spider-Man is currently on $2.4bn worldwide and likely to climb higher, while The Odyssey has made $1.6bn. Other key titles driving sales include Toy Story 5, Michael and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, all of which have grossed over $1bn.

The breadth of the success of Destin Daniel Cretton’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a particular surprise. The film is the best-performing of the year so far and the third highest-grossing film of all time. Its opening weekend was the second-best of all time behind Avengers: Endgame (2019) and it is also the second-fastest film to gross $1bn, doing so in six days.

Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, meanwhile, is the highest-grossing “original” movie of the year, despite its adaptation from Homer’s epic poem. Low-budget original horror movies Backrooms ($394m) and Obsession ($513m) have also helped re-energise the box office.

Sequels and spinoffs accounted for many of the underperformers, including Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu ($345.4m) , Supergirl ($126.4m) and Minions & Monsters ($518.1m – around half of 2022’s Minions: The Rise of Gru).

Meanwhile, August cinema admissions in the UK rose 56% year-on-year to over 17m, according to the UK Cinema Association, signalling the biggest August since 2018 and the second-best performing month since July 2023, when Barbie and Oppenheimer opened together.

Such an uptick is dwarfed by the picture in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, which saw an 88% year-on-year lift, according to Gower Street and the International Union of Cinemas. France’s 19.9m August admissions was the best number recorded during that month since records began 46 years ago, and marked a 50% increase from 2025.

Italian cinemas recorded their best-ever June-August period, with 20.8m admissions and a take of €162.3m, as well as their best ever August. Spain saw a 71% year-on-year increase, while the Netherlands recorded a 77% lift.

articles.title: ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence
articles.text:
On a darkened rooftop in Tel Aviv, Israeli intelligence officers outline the details of their work. These men tell us how they helped develop an AI mapping tool that trawled for phone signals and recommended apartment buildings in Gaza to bomb. Indirectly, they admit, they are responsible for thousands of deaths, but they never spoke up because that wasn’t their place. “My role is technical,” says one. “I’m just a small cog,” says another.

NAZA – directed by the Israeli film-makers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham and produced by the Guardian – is a chilling documentary about a mass slaughter that was authorised at the highest levels of government. But it is also, primarily, about the process, the system, the little links in the killing chain. Szor and Abraham build their film around the accounts of 24 anonymised military and intelligence insiders. NAZA, we learn, is an acronym used by the intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. The Israel Defense Forces prefer to target Hamas terrorists in their homes at night – and if they live with their family, or in heavily populated neighbourhoods, too bad. At one point, a source claims, approval was given to kill 500 NAZA for one Hamas member.

I meet Szor and Abraham at the Venice film festival, where NAZA is competing for the Golden Lion award. The pair won an Oscar for their previous documentary, 2024’s No Other Land (co-directed with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal), which spotlighted Palestinian resistance in the occupied West Bank. “No Other Land documented horrible crimes,” Abraham says. “But at the same time it gave people … I don’t want to say hope, but some light to latch on to. It’s not a coincidence that this film is all in the dark. We are in a very dark place right now.”

The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in three years of Israeli bombardment, the vast majority of which have been civilian casualties. NAZA briefly shows us the rubble, grieving parents, dead children on the ground. Its main backdrop, though, is placid, normal Tel Aviv, just 44 miles to the north, where rush-hour traffic drifts dreamily on the street and the cinematheque is showing a Claude Lanzmann retrospective. Tellingly, the film was executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the director of The Zone of Interest. It was Glazer, says Szor, who advised on the structure and creative approach, fostering the sense of a home that sits next door to a hell.

NAZA deliberately concerns itself with the system – the policy of mass surveillance, the industrial business of murder – more than the individual psychology of those involved. But presumably its sources must feel guilt and shame, otherwise they’d never have agreed to put their careers and liberty at risk.

Abraham is unconvinced. “Well, it depends which one,” he says. “There are many motivations for an individual to speak. Some people talk because they feel the opposite of shame. They feel pride in their accomplishment and expertise. Remember that these people serve in sensitive units. They are not often asked what they do. So there is an attraction to [our] curiosity that drives them to speak up.”

The film uncovers a system that is fiendishly efficient. Its series of disconnects appears designed to distance the perpetrators from the crime. Many of these men work remotely from Tel Aviv. AI selects the target and a drone drops the bomb. Even the language feels purposely euphemistic and obfuscatory. NAZA translates as collateral damage, which in turn translates to human beings.

“Sure, it’s easier to kill people when you’re doing it on a screen,” Abraham says. “There is some truth in that, I guess. But equally it should be said that intelligence officers know the most. They listen to the cellphones. They know the house they are bombing is full of children. They can hear babies crying. They still order another strike.”

What is the status of these men now? Some discuss their work in the past tense. Others don’t, which suggests that they might still be at work, overseeing airstrikes each night. Abraham won’t say; he’s mindful of protecting his sources. “But you can imagine. We are dealing with 24 people, so there is a whole variety of statuses.”

NAZA prompts obvious questions about the creatures of darkness we see on screen. But it prompts intriguing ones, too, about Szor and Abraham, a pair of dissident investigative journalists from the country’s middle class. In the furious, febrile climate of post-7 October Israel, their work is liable to make them pariahs, if not enemies of the state.

Szor jokes that she just wields the camera and therefore keeps out of sight. “Nobody knows who I am, and I’m very happy about that. But some of my family – and some people I’m close to – don’t accept what I do. After the Oscars [last year] they were very ashamed, very angry. But this is a small price to pay.”

Abraham, by contrast, is more vocal and visible. After No Other Land’s premiere at the 2024 Berlin film festival, his family home was targeted by a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he says. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”

Even so, he adds quickly, let’s keep things in perspective. “We’re taking risks in a system that privileges us, that has Jewish-Israeli supremacy as its founding characteristic. So yeah, it was scary for my mum. But she went and slept at my sister’s and her house is still there. For so many Palestinians, it’s not a rightwing mob that’s coming to their home: it’s US-funded bulldozers and weapons. Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials. There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.”

Rooftops at night are a good location, says Szor. They lend themselves to contemplation and help people speak more freely. One soldier recalls the “insane fun” of shooting at people who ran towards a food distribution centre. Another remembers visiting Holocaust sites as a boy and wondering how the German people could have acted as they did. “I still see the Nazis as evil,” he says. “But what does that mean I am?”

After its Venice premiere, NAZA is greeted with a 25-minute ovation. Variety calls it a “devastating exposé” of systematic mass slaughter. The Hollywood Reporter claims that its “bombshell” revelations are likely to provoke outrage and disgust “on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime and its prime minister, Bibi Netanyahu”

(The Israeli military on Friday said it “categorically rejects” the allegations made in the documentary, and criticised the film’s use of anonymous testimonies, which it said “cannot be verified”. In its statement to the Guardian, the IDF said that it “makes unprecedented efforts to minimise harm to civilians” during its offensive in Gaza.)

At the official press conference, the film-makers are asked about parallels between the Holocaust and the killing in Gaza. Abraham points out that this connection was made by one of the soldiers in the film. But he takes the man’s point. “When we say ‘never again’ and that we have to learn from what happened in the Holocaust, the way to do that is to think about patterns that can be seen and observed in the present. I’m not saying [the situation is Gaza] is the same or identical. I don’t think it is. But what we should be doing is recognising these similar patterns of demonisation and killing.”

Who are these men who we can barely see on the screen? The polite data analysts. The soft-spoken officers. Almost all, it turns out, are products of Tel Aviv’s middle class: intelligent, educated and liberal, at least up to a point. Or to put it more bluntly, these are Szor and Abraham’s people. They come from the same neighbourhoods, share similar interests and probably have friends in common. It’s the ultimate paranoid horror trope: the call that comes from inside the house. It shows the extent of the rot and the film-makers’ own proximity to it.

NAZA asks how these men helped kill tens of thousands of civilians. That’s somehow simpler and less frightening than asking why. Abraham shakes his head. “And I have to say I don’t have a clear answer as to why so many people took part in this. And why so few people – in fact, I don’t know of any – refused in real time to do it. It’s scary what that says about the state of Israel. When people talk about genocide, they often speak about it as something that spreads across society, this general atmosphere that normalises death. When everyone else is doing it, it’s easier not to ask questions.”

articles.title: ‘People think fame is a magic wand’: Jarvis Cocker on old songs, young fans and his granny’s verdict on Pulp
articles.text:
When the director Garth Jennings first moved to Paris, Jarvis Cocker, who was living there, dropped in on his old friend. “And I nearly got you arrested,” the Pulp frontman recalls. It was bonfire night, and Cocker had taken some welcoming fireworks over to Jennings’ place. “It turned out Garth’s apartment was quite near to the – not an army base, but what’s it called?”

“The École Militaire,” says Jennings.

“So obviously they didn’t like explosives,” says Cocker. “We got told off for that. The best welcome to Paris.”

“It was lovely,” adds Jennings, fondly. “I remember it very well.”

The men had first met in the late 1990s, when Jennings directed two gorgeous music videos for Pulp, for the singles Help the Aged and A Little Soul. Now, almost 30 years later, they are working together again, on Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? This joyful, funny, celebratory film is a hybrid beast: part concert movie and part documentary on the long history of the band. The live show was filmed at London’s O2 Arena in the summer of 2025, on the night that Pulp were told that More, their eighth studio album and first album in 24 years, had gone to No 1 in the British album charts. You can see Cocker waving around the trophy on stage.

Jennings, director of Son of Rambow and The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, has lived in Paris for the past 13 years, where the animation for Sing, his wildly successful kids’ musical film franchise, is made. He is working on a short Christmas special, and the third and final film in the series. “It’s a slow process,” he says, from the studio, “but we’re getting there.” Cocker moved back to London a few years ago, and today he is at home, getting ready to headline the End of the Road festival. It will be Pulp’s last show for a while.

You can blame Instagram and Abba Voyage for the existence of What Do You Do for an Encore? Pulp, formed by Cocker in Sheffield in 1978, split up in 2002. They got back together for a reunion tour between 2011 and 2013, the final date of which was captured for another idiosyncratic documentary, Florian Habicht’s Pulp: A Film About Life, Death & Supermarkets. Cocker had considered those shows to be a fitting – and final – farewell.

“When Pulp got together that time, I had this idea that things had ended in a not-nice way, and I wanted it to have a happy ending,” Cocker says. “I thought the way to do that would be to play concerts, and we invited Russell Senior back” – the violinist and guitarist had quit in 1997 – “and I just thought it would be like: we’re all friends, everything’s good, and then we’d all retire,” says Cocker. “And to be honest, that tour did seem to do that.”

So when a promoter got in touch years later, to ask if Pulp would be interested in playing again, Cocker had to think about it. “Because the worst thing to do would have been to spoil the happy ending.” How did he decide to say yes? “I confessed my fear that people wouldn’t come, or that people weren’t that bothered, and why would they be?” The promoter assured him that people would most definitely be bothered. “He told me about a few times when he’d been to shows and a Pulp song had come on before a band went on, and everybody sang along. You know, I don’t go to shows any more. I’m an old bloke.” (Cocker is about to turn 63.) “I just said: ‘All right, I hope you’re right, let’s do it.’ But I wanted to make sure that it would be a good thing for us to do as well.”

Cocker teased the news of a second Pulp reunion on Instagram in 2022. Jennings messaged him to tell him how excited he was, and to offer his help. It is obvious, when chatting to Jennings, that as well as being Cocker’s friend, he is a huge Pulp fan. As they started to work on the creative direction of the live show together, Jennings remembers, “I’d be in some other room working on a graphics thing, and then I’d suddenly hear you lot playing, and I’d have to just drop it and come outside. Especially a song like Razzmatazz, which was my first Pulp song. I found you through that. You started playing that at one point, and it was just the best thing ever. I had this wonderful little secret window into this world.”

When it became obvious that the live show was going to be a spectacle, they started to wonder about turning it into a film. “Some of my favourite films are concert films, and they don’t need to be anything more. But this felt like an opportunity to go a bit further,” says Jennings.

Which is where Abba Voyage comes in. Both Jennings and Cocker had seen – and loved – the theatrical experience, which blends live music with giant holograms of Abba in their prime. “That was something that was very inspiring. Just the sheer joy of it,” says Jennings, who has seen it three times. As well as performing the hits, Abba Voyage tells the story of Abba, just as What Do You Do for an Encore? tells the story of Pulp, giving each song context.

“I was so glad when Garth got in touch, because it felt as if he could help make it something that people hadn’t seen before,” Cocker says. “I am very familiar with Pulp’s backstory because I’ve lived through it. But I’m always flabbergasted at how long the band has gone on.” It is clear from the footage of the crowd, showing people losing their minds and singing every word, that some of the audience were not even born when Pulp split up for the first time. “That’s something amazing, really. And something I can’t explain – why young people have latched on to it.” They played in Manchester recently. “A lot of young people,” Cocker laughs. “But I’m happy about it.”

The film uses animation, old TV clips and grainy VHS footage, as well as documents and objects that fans may recognise from Cocker’s 2023 book Good Pop Bad Pop. It was a “huge job” to pull it together, says Jennings, who credits the archivist Tess McNally-Watson with some serious hard work. “Because it’s not all in one place. It’s in people’s bedrooms and attics, and someone’s friend’s brother’s still got a cassette, so it’s a lot of Raiders of the Lost Ark-style gathering and then transferring.” At one point, there is a funny, fond interview with Cocker’s mother and grandmother, who crack jokes about his newfound fame. “That’s a bit embarrassing for me,” says Cocker. “My grandma’s been dead ages, and my mum died only three or four years ago, so it was quite a thing.”

During the live show, Pulp pay a moving tribute to Steve Mackey, who joined the band as bassist in 1989, and who died in 2023 aged 56. Mackey was not going to play on this tour, though he had wished his old bandmates luck. It was important that he was included in the film, and Cocker says that they were able to show it to Mackey’s family before it was signed off. “Just to make sure that they were happy with it. But I think you did a very good job there, Garth. It’s a hard thing to express in the right way.”

What Do You Do for an Encore? does not shy away from the more complicated times in Pulp’s story. Around the release of their then-divisive album This Is Hardcore in 1998, Cocker describes “going down a dark tunnel”. Jennings was making videos for the band back then. Had he noticed that things seemed off?

“I didn’t notice Jarvis going down a dark tunnel, and maybe you were, Jarvis, and I apologise if I wasn’t there to help you,” he says, sincerely. “But no, because the actual act of making these things was always lovely. I never noticed you being tricky, or anything.”

“It was probably because I’d decided to be in a band when I was seven,” Cocker reflects. “Like a lot of people, you think that if you achieve fame, that will be the magic wand that makes everything in your life work, and obviously that’s not the case. You still have to make an effort in your life. You can’t just lie in a bed and say: ‘Right, OK, that’s it, job done.’ But I didn’t realise that, so that’s why I had issues with it.” Over time, he says, “I went back into real life and appreciated it. That was probably another reason why it took me a while to decide to do Pulp again. I was thinking: ‘Well, what’s the motivation? What will you get from it?’”

In the film, Cocker describes Pulp as “scaling Mount Pop”, but it sounds as if he didn’t much like what he found at the summit. “It’s like seeing videos of your wedding. Your wedding is a magical thing, but then somebody shows you a video, and you think: ‘Oh God, what’s that?’” He prefers fantasy to reality, he says, “but sometimes you have to look at reality. And that’s what happened.” Fame, he says, “is an exciting thing, but you just have to keep your wits about you, and make sure you’re doing things for the right reason, and try not to get too up your own arse.”

When he was still at school, in one of his exercise books, Cocker wrote out a “Pulp master plan”. It makes an appearance in the film. But really, he says, they’ve never had one. “I’m glad things that things didn’t go according to a plan. That’s the great thing about groups. You know that you have to work with other people, and everybody adds something to it, and then you get something that you can’t really say exactly where it came from.”

Pulp’s End of the Road set last week marked the end of a tour that started in 2023, though the band are planning to meet up again in October, to celebrate it all. They’re going to see Abba Voyage together. Will there be another encore? “You know, it’s like a tree,” says Cocker, philosophically. “A tree doesn’t decide it’s going to grow. If the weather’s right, it’ll grow a branch. And if the intellectual weather is right in the next couple of years, maybe we’ll sprout another record.” He said it himself: there has never been a master plan.

Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? is on Mubi from 25 September, with special one night only preview screenings at UK and Irish cinemas on 18 September and in US cinemas on 24 September
